docs.title: 3.5 Chillers, Cooling Towers & Refrigerants
docs.text:
In bigger data centres the heat collected from the halls is carried away by water pipes to a central plant. A chiller uses a refrigeration cycle (like a giant fridge) to make cold water, and then dumps the heat outside through fans or a cooling tower. Pumps move the water around, and the refrigerant gases inside chillers are now tightly regulated because many of them warm the planet.

The vapour-compression refrigeration cycle. Heat enters at the evaporator and leaves at the condenser; the compressor pays for the lift between them.

Think of it like…

A chiller plant is the heart and lungs of the building: pumps push cold water out to the halls like blood, and the cooling towers 'breathe out' the collected heat to the sky.

Real-world example

The fictional Meridian Cloud campus has a 4 MW data hall served by three 2 MW water-cooled chillers (N+1). Chilled water leaves at 18 °C and returns at 26 °C; at an 8 °C delta-T, 4 MW needs about 120 litres per second of flow. The condenser side sends heat to cooling towers on the roof. When the operator upgrades to magnetic-bearing compressors and a low-GWP refrigerant, chiller energy at part load falls noticeably and the site is ready for tighter refrigerant rules.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. CRAHs, in-row units or CDUs pass heat from the hall into a chilled-water loop.
  2. Pumps (usually on VFDs) send the warmed water back to the chillers.
  3. In each chiller, refrigerant evaporates to absorb the heat; a compressor raises its pressure and temperature.
  4. The hot refrigerant gives up its heat in the condenser, to outside air (air-cooled) or condenser water and a cooling tower (water-cooled).
  5. Controls stage chillers, pumps and towers on and off to match the load at the lowest energy.

Who uses it

Chief engineers, chiller technicians, HVAC contractors and refrigeration engineers run and maintain these plants; F-gas certified technicians are needed to handle refrigerants.

Key takeaway

Remember the water equation: kW = flow (L/s) x 4.186 x delta-T (°C); doubling delta-T halves the pumping flow you need.

Going deeper

  • Efficiency converts as kW/ton = 3.517 / COP, so a COP of 7 equals about 0.5 kW/ton; plant-level figures add pumps and tower fans to the chiller itself.
  • Compressor work depends on lift, the gap between evaporating and condensing temperatures; supplying chilled water at 18-20 °C instead of 7 °C cuts lift and energy substantially.
  • AHRI 550/590's IPLV weights efficiency at 100, 75, 50 and 25% load by 1, 42, 45 and 12%, reflecting that chillers spend most hours at part load.
  • Low delta-T syndrome occurs when water returns too cool, forcing extra pumps and chillers to run; causes include bypass valves, fouled coils and oversupplied air.
  • Refrigerant GWP matters: R-134a is about 1,430, R-513A about 630, R-454B about 470 and R-1234ze below 1, so newer gases sharply cut leakage impact.
  • The US AIM Act phases HFC production down by 85% by 2036, and the EU F-gas Regulation 2024/573 phases HFCs out by 2050.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Supplying 7 °C chilled water out of habit; it wastes energy, dehumidifies needlessly and causes condensation on pipes.
  • Assuming N+1 chillers guarantee cooling; restart time, shared pumps, controls and a single header can still be single points of failure.
  • Neglecting condenser-water treatment; scaled or fouled tubes quietly raise kW/ton and can trip chillers on high pressure.

docs.title: Try it: Python: chilled-water flow needed for a heat load
docs.text:
load_kw = 4000          # heat to remove
supply_c, return_c = 18, 26

dt = return_c - supply_c
flow_ls = load_kw / (4.186 * dt)      # 1 litre of water ~ 1 kg
print(f'Delta-T {dt} C -> {flow_ls:.0f} L/s ({flow_ls*3.6:.0f} m3/h)')
print(f'Chiller capacity needed: {load_kw/3.517:.0f} tons of refrigeration')

docs.title: 3.6 Economisers & Free Cooling
docs.text:
When the weather outside is cooler than the data hall needs, you can use outside air or cold water to do the cooling and switch the power-hungry compressors off. This is called free cooling, and the equipment that does it is an economiser. The colder and drier the climate, the more hours per year a site can run this way.

Three ways to cool for free

Direct air Indirect air Water-side Outside air enters hall? Yes, filtered No, heat exchanger No Heat path Outside air replaces hall air Air-to-air heat exchanger Tower or dry cooler + plate HX Limited by Temperature, humidity, pollution Dry-bulb (wet-bulb if sprayed) Wet-bulb or dry-bulb Main risks Smoke, dust, humidity swings Large footprint Freezing, approach losses Typical user Hyperscale in cool climates Colo and hyperscale Chilled-water plants

The warmer your supply setpoint, the more hours each option can run without compressors.

Think of it like…

Free cooling is like opening the window on a cool evening instead of running the air conditioner.

Real-world example

The fictional Fjordline Data site in Norway sets its supply air to 24 °C. Because outdoor air is below about 20 °C for most of the year, its indirect air economiser runs with compressors off for over 90% of hours. A sister site in Madrid with the same design gets far fewer free-cooling hours and runs its mechanical cooling much more in summer. The Norwegian site's PUE is consequently lower, showing how climate shapes design.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Compare outside conditions with the required supply temperature (warmer setpoints mean more free-cooling hours).
  2. If outside air or water is cold enough, use it alone (full free cooling) and turn compressors off.
  3. If it is only partly cold enough, pre-cool with the economiser and let chillers top up (partial free cooling).
  4. When it is too hot or humid, switch to mechanical cooling or evaporative assistance.
  5. Use weather data (hourly bin data) during design to estimate annual free-cooling hours and energy savings.

Who uses it

Mechanical designers, energy engineers and site selection teams use economiser analysis; operators tune changeover points every season.

Key takeaway

Key interview point: raising the supply temperature within the ASHRAE range is what unlocks more economiser hours.

Going deeper

  • Approaches stack up: with an 18 °C supply target, a 4 °C tower approach and a 2 °C heat-exchanger approach, full water-side free cooling needs wet-bulb at or below about 12 °C.
  • Energy codes such as ASHRAE 90.1 and 90.4 require or credit economisers in many climate zones, so most new designs include one.
  • Direct air systems need dampers that close and mechanical backup ready for wildfire smoke, pollen or pollution events that can arrive within minutes.
  • Partial (integrated) free cooling still saves energy when outdoor conditions are only a little colder than return water, which adds many hours in temperate climates.
  • Raising supply temperature within the ASHRAE recommended range is the main lever; a few degrees can add thousands of economiser hours per year in temperate climates.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Designing from typical weather instead of extremes; plant must still cope on a record heatwave day with free cooling unavailable.
  • Poorly tuned changeover that makes chillers short-cycle on and off during mild spring and autumn afternoons.
  • Assuming free cooling costs nothing; fans, pumps, filters and water treatment still use energy and money.

docs.title: Try it: Python: count free-cooling hours from a list of hourly outdoor temperatures
docs.text:
import random
random.seed(1)
# fake year of hourly temperatures for a mild climate
hours = [10 + 10*random.random() + 8*random.uniform(-1, 1) for _ in range(8760)]
supply_setpoint = 24
approach = 4   # heat exchanger needs outdoor air ~4 C colder than supply

free = sum(1 for t in hours if t <= supply_setpoint - approach)
print(f'Free-cooling hours: {free} of 8760 ({free/87.6:.0f}%)')

docs.title: 3.7 Evaporative & Adiabatic Cooling and Water Use
docs.text:
Evaporating water absorbs a lot of heat, which is why you feel cold when you step out of a swimming pool. Many data centres use this effect to cool air or water cheaply, but it consumes large amounts of water. Operators now balance energy savings against water use, especially in dry regions, and some new designs avoid evaporating water at all.

Where cooling-tower water goes. Evaporation does the cooling; blowdown and drift are the extra water you also pay for.

Think of it like…

An evaporative cooler works like sweat on your skin: water evaporates, takes heat with it, and leaves you cooler.

Real-world example

The fictional Cedar Valley campus in a dry US state uses cooling towers that evaporate about 1.5 litres of water for every kWh of heat removed, plus extra 'blowdown' water to flush out minerals. Local residents raise concerns during a drought. For its next building the operator switches to dry coolers with adiabatic pads used only on the hottest days and to warm-water liquid cooling. Water use falls sharply, while annual energy use rises slightly.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Warm, dry air passes over wet media or through a fine water spray.
  2. Water evaporates, absorbing latent heat and cooling the air (direct) or a separate air stream (indirect).
  3. In cooling towers the same effect cools condenser water instead of air.
  4. Minerals left behind are flushed out as blowdown, and the water is treated against scale, corrosion and Legionella.
  5. Water use is tracked with meters and reported as WUE (litres per kWh of IT energy).

Who uses it

Mechanical engineers, water-treatment contractors, sustainability managers and local planners all care about data-centre water use.

Key takeaway

Rule of thumb: evaporating 1 litre of water removes roughly 0.65 kWh of heat, so heat rejected purely by evaporation uses about 1.5 L per kWh of heat.

Going deeper

  • Blowdown equals evaporation divided by (cycles of concentration minus 1): at 4 cycles, blowdown is a third of evaporation; at 6 cycles it falls to a fifth.
  • Direct evaporative media typically achieve about 80-90% of the gap between dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperature, so dry climates gain the most.
  • Legionella grows best between about 20 and 45 °C, exactly the range of many towers; water safety plans follow ASHRAE Standard 188 or the UK HSE L8 code.
  • Site WUE ignores water consumed by power stations; a dry-cooled site with higher PUE may use more total water once the electricity's source water is counted.
  • Hybrid and adiabatic systems run dry for most hours and wet only on hot days, often cutting annual water use dramatically versus open towers.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Estimating water use from evaporation alone; blowdown and drift can add a third or more on top.
  • Comparing sites on site WUE alone while ignoring the extra electricity, and power-station water, a water-free design may need.
  • Leaving adiabatic pads wet or poorly maintained; scale and stagnant water create Legionella and performance problems.

docs.title: Try it: Python: estimate annual evaporation and WUE for a cooling tower site
docs.text:
it_mwh_year = 10 * 8760          # 10 MW IT running all year
heat_mwh = it_mwh_year * 1.05    # IT heat plus a little extra
evap_share = 0.5                 # fraction of hours using evaporation
litres_per_kwh_heat = 3600 / 2400   # latent heat ~2,400 kJ/kg at tower temperatures

evap_l = heat_mwh * 1000 * evap_share * litres_per_kwh_heat
blowdown_l = evap_l / 3          # ~4 cycles of concentration
wue = (evap_l + blowdown_l) / (it_mwh_year * 1000)
print(f'Water: {(evap_l+blowdown_l)/1e6:,.0f} million litres/year, WUE ~ {wue:.2f} L/kWh')

docs.title: 3.8 Direct-to-Chip Liquid Cooling and CDUs
docs.text:
Direct-to-chip cooling bolts small metal blocks called cold plates onto the hottest chips, and pumps liquid through them to carry the heat away. A coolant distribution unit (CDU) controls this liquid loop and passes the heat to the building's main water system. It is now the standard way to cool high-power AI and HPC servers.

Inside a coolant distribution unit. The CDU isolates clean server coolant from building water while controlling flow, pressure and temperature.

Think of it like…

A cold plate is like holding an ice pack directly on a sprained ankle instead of turning down the room temperature: the cooling goes straight to where the heat is.

Real-world example

The fictional research lab Aurora HPC installs 40 GPU racks at 80 kW each. Cold plates on the GPUs and CPUs capture about 80% of the heat into a PG25 loop, and two in-row CDUs pass it to 32 °C facility water through plate heat exchangers. The remaining heat from memory, drives and power supplies is handled by existing CRAHs. Leak-detection cable under each rack and dripless quick disconnects let technicians swap servers safely.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Cold plates with tiny internal channels sit on CPUs and GPUs, replacing traditional heatsinks.
  2. Coolant flows from rack manifolds through hoses and quick disconnects to each server, collecting heat.
  3. The CDU pumps the coolant (the technology cooling system, TCS) and filters it.
  4. A heat exchanger in the CDU transfers the heat to the facility water system (FWS).
  5. Sensors watch flow, pressure, temperature and leaks, and the CDU adjusts pumps and valves automatically.

Who uses it

Liquid-cooling engineers, HPC and AI infrastructure teams, mechanical contractors and data-centre technicians work with DLC every day in AI factories and supercomputing centres.

Key takeaway

Learn the two loops: TCS (the clean coolant to the servers) and FWS (the building water), joined by the CDU's heat exchanger — interviewers often ask this.

Going deeper

  • Cold plates capture most but not all heat; AI servers often send 80% or more to liquid, leaving memory, NICs, drives and power supplies for air cooling.
  • The CDU heat exchanger has an approach of a few degrees, so TCS supply runs slightly warmer than facility water; this must be included when choosing an ASHRAE W class.
  • Glycol mixtures protect against freezing and microbes but lower specific heat and raise viscosity, so PG25 needs more flow and pump power than treated water.
  • Wetted materials such as copper, stainless steel and EPDM must be compatible with the coolant; mixing in aluminium without inhibitors invites galvanic corrosion.
  • Each cold plate, hose and quick disconnect adds pressure drop; manifolds are designed so every server gets its share of flow, and CDUs control differential pressure.
  • OCP's cooling work publishes open specifications, such as UQD couplings and Google's Project Deschutes CDU, to make components interchangeable across vendors.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming liquid cooling removes the need for air; residual heat from a 130 kW rack can still be 15-25 kW.
  • Running a single CDU for many racks without redundant pumps or a backup unit, making it a single point of failure.
  • Skipping coolant sampling; inhibitor depletion and bacteria slowly corrode and clog cold plates.
  • Letting untrained staff disconnect hoses; only rated dripless quick disconnects and a written procedure should be used.

docs.title: Try it: Python: how much coolant flow does a liquid-cooled rack need?
docs.text:
rack_kw = 80
liquid_capture = 0.80          # share of heat into cold plates
cp_pg25 = 3.9                  # kJ/kgK, roughly, for 25% propylene glycol
dt = 10                        # coolant temperature rise in C

q_liquid = rack_kw * liquid_capture
flow_kgs = q_liquid / (cp_pg25 * dt)
print(f'Liquid heat: {q_liquid:.0f} kW, flow ~ {flow_kgs*60:.0f} L/min')
print(f'Air heat left for room cooling: {rack_kw - q_liquid:.0f} kW')

docs.title: 3.9 Rear-Door Heat Exchangers and Liquid-to-Air Retrofits
docs.text:
A rear-door heat exchanger replaces the back door of a rack with a radiator full of cool water, so hot exhaust air is cooled before it ever reaches the room. Related 'liquid-to-air' units let a data hall without building water pipes still run some liquid-cooled servers. These are popular ways to add density to existing halls without rebuilding them.

Three retrofit options

Passive rear door Active rear door Liquid-to-air sidecar Fans None, server fans push air Fans in the door Fans in the unit Needs facility water Yes Yes No Typical rack density Up to roughly 20-30 kW Higher, 40 kW and more A few liquid-cooled servers Heat ends up in Water loop Water loop Room air, then existing coolers Best use Moderate density uplift Dense air-cooled racks Pilot DLC in an air-only hall

Rear doors still need water; a sidecar needs none but dumps the heat back into the room.

Think of it like…

A rear-door heat exchanger is like a cold, wet towel hanging over the back of a hairdryer: the hot blast is cooled the moment it leaves.

Real-world example

The fictional Lakeside University wants five 35 kW AI racks in a hall designed for 8 kW. Instead of rebuilding cooling for the whole room, it fits active rear-door heat exchangers fed by a small CDU from the existing chilled-water loop. Exhaust air leaves the doors at almost room temperature. A year later, when two liquid-cooled GPU servers arrive, a liquid-to-air sidecar unit cools their cold plates without new outdoor plant.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Servers blow hot exhaust out of their backs as usual.
  2. The air passes through a water coil in the rack's rear door.
  3. In passive doors, server fans alone push the air; in active doors, extra fans in the door help.
  4. Water (via a CDU, kept above dew point) carries the heat back to the chilled-water or facility loop.
  5. For cold-plate servers in air-only halls, a liquid-to-air CDU rejects the coolant heat into the room or containment instead.

Who uses it

Operations engineers, colocation providers and universities use rear doors and sidecars to upgrade older halls for AI and HPC.

Key takeaway

Passive rear doors typically suit up to roughly 20-30 kW per rack, while active doors handle more; always keep door water above the room dew point to avoid condensation.

Going deeper

  • Door capacity depends on water temperature and flow, and on how hot the server exhaust is; hotter exhaust and colder water both increase heat removed.
  • Door water is usually supplied through a liquid-to-liquid CDU that holds it above the room dew point while building chilled water may be colder.
  • A room-neutral door returns air at about inlet temperature, but the room still needs some air handling for humidity, people and any residual heat.
  • Liquid-to-air sidecars move cold-plate heat into the room, so they only make sense when room cooling has spare capacity; they do not reduce facility cooling load.
  • Doors are heavy when full of water; check hinge clearances, aisle width, floor loading and hose routing before ordering.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming a liquid-to-air sidecar reduces facility cooling load; the heat still ends up in the room air.
  • Letting door water fall below the room dew point; condensation drips onto equipment and floors.
  • Fitting passive doors without checking server fan back-pressure and the vendor's airflow approval.

Close-coupled rear doors let one dense row run without changing cooling for the rest of the hall. Engineers confirm the server maker approves the door's pressure drop before fitting passive doors.

docs.title: 3.10 Immersion Cooling
docs.text:
Immersion cooling dunks whole servers into a tank of special liquid that does not conduct electricity, so the liquid touches every hot part directly. In single-phase systems the liquid stays liquid and is pumped to a heat exchanger; in two-phase systems it boils on the chips and condenses on a cold coil above. It removes heat very efficiently and needs no server fans, but it changes how servers are handled and maintained.

Single-phase vs two-phase immersion

Single-phase Two-phase Fluid state Stays liquid, pumped Boils on chips, condenses on coil Typical fluids Synthetic hydrocarbons, esters Engineered fluorinated fluids Heat transfer Forced convection Boiling, nearly constant temperature Fluid loss Low volatility, drips Vapour escapes if tank opened Regulatory risk Low High (PFAS restrictions) Maturity Commercially established Emerging, niche

Two-phase moves heat brilliantly but its fluids face PFAS rules and vapour losses.

Think of it like…

Single-phase immersion is like cooling a hot frying pan by lowering it into a sink of water, except the 'water' here is a safe oil that will not short anything.

Real-world example

The fictional crypto-to-AI company Polar Compute runs 24 immersion tanks, each holding about 50 kW of servers in synthetic hydrocarbon fluid. Pumps move warm fluid at around 45 °C to heat exchangers, and the heat goes to dry coolers with no water evaporation. Server fans were removed, saving several percent of IT power. Technicians use an overhead lift and drip trays when pulling servers, and they must check that every component (including cable glue and labels) is compatible with the fluid.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Servers (often with fans removed) are placed vertically into a tank filled with dielectric fluid.
  2. Single-phase: fluid absorbs heat, is pumped to a heat exchanger, cooled and returned.
  3. Two-phase: fluid boils on hot chips, vapour rises to a condenser coil, turns back to liquid and drips down.
  4. The heat exchanger passes the heat to facility water, then to dry coolers, towers or a heat-reuse network.
  5. Maintenance uses lifts, drip racks and fluid top-ups, with regular fluid quality checks.

Who uses it

Specialist cooling engineers, crypto-mining and HPC operators, edge-site designers and some AI cloud providers use immersion; it is less common than direct-to-chip in large AI halls.

Key takeaway

Know the PFAS story: 3M exited PFAS manufacturing (including Novec and Fluorinert fluids) by the end of 2025, pushing two-phase immersion towards newer fluids.

Going deeper

  • Servers for immersion usually lose their fans and may need fluid-compatible thermal interface materials, labels and cable jackets that will not dissolve or leach.
  • Tanks are horizontal baths with servers inserted vertically from above, so floor layout, lifting gear and service clearances differ completely from rack rows.
  • Single-phase fluids are monitored for contamination, oxidation and dielectric strength, and are filtered continuously; good fluids can last many years.
  • Immersion heat leaves at relatively warm temperatures, which suits dry coolers and heat reuse and removes the need for evaporative cooling in most climates.
  • Open Compute Project working groups publish immersion requirements so server makers, fluid suppliers and tank vendors can design to a shared baseline.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming any server can be immersed; check warranty support, hard drives, optics and every material against the chosen fluid.
  • Forgetting floor loading and spill containment; a full tank holds hundreds of litres of fluid.
  • Treating two-phase immersion as the obvious future without weighing PFAS restrictions, fluid cost and vapour losses.

docs.title: 3.11 Heat Reuse & District Heating
docs.text:
All the heat a data centre removes is normally thrown away into the air. Heat reuse captures it and sends it to homes, offices, greenhouses or swimming pools, usually through a district heating network of hot-water pipes. Heat pumps often boost the temperature, and some countries now require new data centres to plan for or deliver heat reuse.

From GPU heat to a warm home. The warmer the heat leaves the data centre, the smaller the heat-pump lift and the cheaper the heat.

Think of it like…

Heat reuse is like using the warm water from your shower to pre-heat the next person's water instead of letting it all go down the drain.

Real-world example

The fictional town of Vellby builds a 20 MW data centre next to its district heating plant. Warm water from the liquid-cooled halls at about 35 °C is boosted by heat pumps to 70 °C and fed into the town network. In winter it supplies a large share of the town's heating demand, and the operator earns income from the heat sale. Its Energy Reuse Factor rises to 0.2, helping it meet national rules.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Collect waste heat at the warmest point available (liquid-cooling return water is warmer than hall air).
  2. Use a heat exchanger to pass the heat into a separate network loop.
  3. Raise the temperature with heat pumps if the network needs hotter water.
  4. Pipe the heat to users such as district heating, buildings, greenhouses or industry.
  5. Measure delivered heat and report metrics such as ERF to regulators and customers.

Who uses it

Sustainability managers, energy engineers, city planners and district heating companies work together on heat-reuse projects, especially in Northern Europe.

Key takeaway

Remember the Energy Reuse Factor (ERF): reused energy divided by total data-centre energy; Germany's EnEfG sets rising ERF targets for new sites.

Going deeper

  • Heat-pump efficiency falls as lift grows; ideal COP is T_hot ÷ (T_hot − T_cold) in kelvin, and real machines reach roughly half of that or less.
  • Heat demand is seasonal: in summer most heat cannot be sold, so the data centre must keep full heat-rejection capacity regardless of any reuse deal.
  • Contracts define temperature, volume, availability and who provides backup; utilities keep boilers for times the data centre cannot deliver.
  • Air-cooled halls offer only around 25-35 °C exhaust heat, while warm-water liquid cooling can return 40-60 °C, making reuse far more economic.
  • The EU Energy Efficiency Directive expects sites over 1 MW to use waste heat unless technically or economically unfeasible, and Germany's EnEfG adds hard ERF quotas.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming waste heat is free money; it needs a nearby buyer, pipes, heat pumps and a long-term contract.
  • Designing heat reuse as the only heat-rejection path; summer demand collapses and the network may be offline for maintenance.
  • Promising high temperatures from air-cooled halls; low-grade heat needs costly heat-pump lift.

docs.title: 3.12 CFD Modelling, Digital Twins & Thermal Monitoring
docs.text:
Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) uses a computer to simulate how air or liquid flows and where it gets hot, before you move a single rack. A digital twin is a living 3D model of the real hall that is kept up to date with sensor data. Together with sensors and dashboards, these tools help teams find hot spots, plan new equipment and save energy.

Keeping a digital twin honest. A model is only trusted after it has been calibrated against real sensor data, and kept updated.

Think of it like…

CFD is like a weather forecast for the inside of your data hall: it predicts where the 'heatwaves' will be so you can act before they happen.

Real-world example

Before installing ten 40 kW racks, the fictional colo Westbridge Data builds a CFD model of Hall 3 from its floor plans and sensor history. The simulation shows that the new row would starve two existing rows of cold air. Engineers test three layouts virtually and pick one with an extra in-row cooler and containment. After installation, measured inlet temperatures match the model within about 1 °C.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Build a model of the room: walls, racks, coolers, floor tiles, cable trays and obstructions.
  2. Add heat loads and airflows for each rack and cooling unit.
  3. Run the simulation to predict temperatures, pressures and airflow paths.
  4. Calibrate the model with real sensor readings so it matches reality.
  5. Test 'what-if' scenarios (new racks, cooler failures) and keep the twin updated as the hall changes.

Who uses it

CFD engineers, capacity planners, DCIM administrators and design consultants use these tools; operations teams rely on the sensor dashboards every shift.

Key takeaway

A CFD model is only as good as its calibration; always compare predictions with measured inlet temperatures before trusting it.

Going deeper

  • CFD divides the room into millions of small cells (the mesh) and solves airflow and heat equations; boundary conditions such as rack airflow and cooler output drive the result.
  • Steady-state runs show normal conditions; transient runs show how quickly temperatures rise after failures, which is critical for dense AI racks.
  • The usual sources of error are floor-tile leakage, unknown rack airflow, missing blanking panels and underfloor obstructions; surveys feed these into the model.
  • Liquid-cooled halls also need hydraulic (1D flow network) models of pipes, CDUs and manifolds, alongside air CFD for the residual heat.
  • Digital twins pull live data from BMS, DCIM and sensors through APIs, so capacity planners can test changes against current conditions instead of design drawings.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Trusting an uncalibrated model; always compare predictions with measured inlet temperatures first.
  • Modelling racks at nameplate power, which exaggerates heat and hides where real problems are.
  • Treating the twin as a one-off project; without updates after every change it drifts from reality within months.

docs.title: Try it: CSV snippet: rack inlet sensor readings and a quick hotspot check in Python
docs.text:
import csv, io
data = '''rack,top_c,mid_c,bottom_c
A01,24.1,22.8,21.5
A02,28.6,24.0,21.9
A03,23.5,22.2,21.0
'''
for row in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(data)):

docs.title: 3.13 Cooling AI and GPU Racks
docs.text:
AI training servers pack dozens of powerful GPUs into one rack, pushing heat output above 100 kW, which is ten or more times a normal rack. Air alone cannot carry that much heat, so these racks are cooled mostly by liquid through cold plates, with a little air for the remaining parts. New GPU generations are designed to accept warmer water, which saves energy and makes heat reuse easier.

Rack density keeps climbing. Each step up needs a different cooling method; air runs out somewhere around 30-50 kW.

Think of it like…

Cooling a modern AI rack with air is like trying to cool a pizza oven with a desk fan; you need to plumb in water to keep up.

Real-world example

The fictional AI start-up Lumen Labs leases a hall for 32 GPU racks of the NVL72 type, each drawing about 130 kW. Most of each rack's heat goes to cold plates on a liquid loop fed by in-row CDUs, while CRAHs remove the leftover air-side heat. Facility water is supplied warm, so dry coolers handle most of the year without chillers. Before go-live, the team tests what happens if a CDU pump fails and confirms the standby pump takes over within seconds.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Find the rack's total power and its liquid-to-air split from the vendor's specification.
  2. Size CDUs and facility water for the liquid share, including redundancy (for example N+1 pumps).
  3. Provide air cooling for the remaining heat from power supplies, network cards and drives.
  4. Choose facility water temperature (warmer water means more free cooling and easier heat reuse).
  5. Design for heavier racks, larger pipes, leak detection and pumps on UPS so cooling survives power events.

Who uses it

AI infrastructure architects, hyperscale and neocloud design teams, colocation engineers and GPU cluster operators work on these designs today.

Key takeaway

Know the trend: NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 racks are roughly 120 kW and liquid cooled, and NVIDIA states 45 °C inlet water for its Vera Rubin NVL72 platform.

Going deeper

  • Per-GPU power has climbed from about 700 W for an H100 SXM module to over 1,000 W for Blackwell-generation GPUs, multiplied by 72 GPUs in one rack.
  • NVIDIA's 800 V DC power architecture targets 1 MW IT racks from 2027, moving power conversion into sidecar racks and leaving more room for liquid-cooled compute.
  • Warm facility water, up to the 45 °C NVIDIA quotes for Vera Rubin, lets dry coolers reject heat most of the year and makes heat reuse easier.
  • Thermal mass in GPU racks is tiny; without coolant flow, chips can reach throttling temperatures within seconds, so CDU pumps and controls sit on UPS.
  • Hybrid halls are normal: liquid for GPU racks, air for storage, networking and the residual 10-20% of GPU rack heat.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Designing for average density rather than the peak racks that will actually arrive; AI halls must plan for the densest generation.
  • Forgetting the residual air-side load of liquid-cooled racks when sizing CRAHs or fan walls.
  • Leaving CDU pumps off UPS; a generator start gap can overheat GPUs before power returns.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Data Centre Foundations
docs.text: Before you study power, cooling or AI clusters, you need the big picture: what a data centre is, the different kinds, the rooms inside, and how power, cooling and data flow through the building. This chapter starts from zero and builds the vocabulary every newcomer needs, from tiers and the 'nines' of availability to PUE, kilowatts and site selection. It ends by following a single app request through a data centre and explaining why AI is reshaping the whole industry.

docs.title: 1.1 What Is a Data Centre and Why Does It Exist?
docs.text:
A data centre is a building, or a dedicated part of a building, built to hold large numbers of computers called servers, plus the storage and network equipment that goes with them. It keeps all that equipment powered, cool, connected to the internet and physically secure, every minute of every day. Almost everything you do online, from sending a message to asking an AI chatbot a question, is processed inside one.

What every data centre provides. Running out of any one resource caps growth, even if the others are spare.

Think of it like…

A data centre is to a home computer what a restaurant kitchen is to your kitchen at home: industrial power, serious ventilation, strict safety rules and staff on every shift so it can serve thousands of people without stopping.

Real-world example

Riverside Credit Union, a fictional small bank, kept its 12 servers in a cupboard behind reception. In one year a heatwave overheated the room and a three-hour power cut took online banking offline twice. The bank moved the servers into two rented racks in a professional data centre 20 km away, with backup generators, proper cooling and guards on duty 24/7. Over the next three years it had no outages caused by power or cooling.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Electricity arrives from the public grid and is backed up by batteries and diesel generators.
  2. Servers, storage and network switches are mounted in standard metal racks inside a secure room.
  3. Cooling systems remove the heat that every watt of electricity eventually turns into.
  4. Fibre-optic cables link the building to internet carriers, cloud providers and other data centres.
  5. Staff, sensors and software watch everything around the clock and fix problems before users notice.

Who uses it

Every bank, hospital, retailer, government, streaming service and AI company depends on data centres, whether it owns them or rents space and computing from someone else.

Key takeaway

Memorise the four basic things every data centre sells or provides: space, power, cooling and connectivity, all wrapped in security and 24/7 operations.

Going deeper

  • Size is quoted in megawatts of critical IT load, not floor area: an enterprise room may be under 1 MW, colocation buildings 5-50 MW, and hyperscale or AI campuses hundreds of MW.
  • Nearly all electricity entering IT equipment leaves as heat, so power and cooling capacity are always designed as a matched pair; the extra energy for cooling and electrical losses shows up in PUE.
  • Standards define the term formally: ANSI/TIA-942 and EN 50600 / ISO/IEC 22237 describe a building housing centralised IT plus its supporting power, environmental control, cabling and security infrastructure.
  • The IEA estimated data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024, around 1.5% of world electricity, with the United States, China and Europe accounting for most of it.
  • Ownership and operation are often split: a developer owns the building, a colocation provider operates it and dozens of tenants own the servers, each with separate contracts and responsibilities.
  • Downtime is expensive: Uptime Institute surveys repeatedly find many significant outages cost well over US$100,000, which is why owners pay for redundancy, monitoring and trained 24/7 staff.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking 'the cloud' is abstract: every cloud service runs on physical servers in real buildings with real power, cooling and staff.
  • Measuring a data centre by floor area: megawatts of IT load are the true size and usually the limiting resource.
  • Calling an office server cupboard a data centre: without backup power, proper cooling and 24/7 monitoring it is a single point of failure.

docs.title: Try it: Estimate how much electricity a small group of servers uses in a year (Python)
docs.text:
watts_per_server = 400      # example average draw of one busy 1U server
servers = 20
hours_per_year = 24 * 365
kwh = watts_per_server * servers * hours_per_year / 1000
print(f"{kwh:,.0f} kWh per year")   # 70,080 kWh
print(f"About {kwh/2700:.0f} typical homes' worth")  # assuming ~2,700 kWh per home per year

docs.title: 1.2 Types of Data Centre
docs.text:
Not all data centres are alike. Some are owned by one company for its own use, some rent space to many customers, and some are giant campuses run by cloud and internet companies. Others are tiny sites close to users, factory-built boxes, or new 'AI factories' packed with graphics processors.

Who owns what?

Enterprise Colocation Cloud / hyperscale Building owner The organisation Provider Provider IT owner The organisation Customer Provider Customer buys Everything Space, power, cooling Compute as a service Typical contract Capital project Monthly or multi-year lease Pay per use Typical size Often under 10 MW One rack to 50 MW+ 100 MW+ campuses

The key question is who owns the building and who owns the servers inside it.

Think of it like…

Data centres are like places to live: you can own a house (enterprise), rent a flat in a block (retail colocation), lease a whole building (wholesale), stay in a hotel where everything is provided (cloud), or park a camper van near where you need to be (edge).

Real-world example

Northgate Retail, a fictional chain, keeps its old payroll system in its own on-premises server hall, rents two cages in a colocation site for its online shop, and runs analytics in a public cloud region. For in-store video analytics it places a small edge cabinet in its regional warehouse to cut delay to under 5 milliseconds. To train a product-recommendation model it rents GPU time from a specialist AI cloud for six weeks.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide who owns the building and who owns the IT equipment inside it.
  2. Enterprise sites: one organisation owns and uses everything.
  3. Colocation: a provider owns the building, power and cooling; customers bring their own IT.
  4. Cloud and hyperscale: the provider owns everything and rents out computing as a service.
  5. Edge, modular and AI sites are chosen for location, speed of deployment or extreme density.

Who uses it

Business leaders, IT managers and procurement teams choose between these models; data centre staff work across all of them.

Key takeaway

In interviews, be able to explain the difference between retail and wholesale colocation, and between a cloud region and an availability zone.

Going deeper

  • Retail colocation is sold by the rack, cage or kW with monthly fees and cross-connect charges; wholesale is sold by the megawatt or whole hall, often on 10-15 year leases to hyperscale tenants.
  • A cloud region holds several availability zones; AWS, for example, describes its zones as physically separated by a meaningful distance yet within about 100 km (60 miles) of each other.
  • Edge sites trade scale for proximity: placing compute within a few tens of kilometres of users cuts round-trip delay to a few milliseconds, useful for gaming, video analytics and 5G services.
  • Hyperscalers both build their own campuses and lease large wholesale capacity, so one hall can be 'colocation' to the developer and 'cloud' to the end customer.
  • AI-focused facilities differ mainly in density: liquid-cooled GPU racks of 100 kW or more, heavier floors, larger power blocks and very fast cluster networks.
  • Modular and prefabricated designs cut build time by factory-testing power skids, cooling modules or whole IT pods, then assembling them on site in parallel with civil works.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Confusing colocation with cloud: in colocation you own and manage the servers; in cloud you rent computing and never touch the hardware.
  • Assuming every hyperscale hall is owned by the cloud company: many are leased from wholesale developers under build-to-suit deals.
  • Treating availability zones as disaster recovery in distant cities: zones in one region are relatively close; true DR needs a second region.

docs.title: 1.3 Anatomy of a Data Centre: The Rooms and Spaces
docs.text:
A data centre is not one big room of computers. The 'white space' holds the IT racks, while the 'grey space' holds the electrical and cooling machinery that keeps them alive. Around these sit rooms for network connections, security, deliveries, monitoring staff, spares and backup generators.

Spaces around the data hall. Grey space and support rooms can take as much floor area as the white space they serve.

Think of it like…

Think of a theatre: the stage is the white space where the show happens, while backstage (grey space) holds the lighting rigs, power and crew that make the show possible.

Real-world example

On her first day at a fictional 12 MW site, technician Amara is badged through the guardhouse and a two-door security airlock. She is shown four data halls of 3 MW each, a UPS and battery room behind each hall, the generator yard with eight diesel generators, and two meet-me rooms where carriers connect. Deliveries arrive at the loading dock, and new servers are unboxed in the build room so cardboard never enters the data hall.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pass the perimeter fence and guardhouse, then a mantrap or airlock into the building.
  2. Deliveries go via the loading dock to a staging or build room, never straight into the halls.
  3. Data halls (white space) hold rows of racks in hot and cold aisles.
  4. Electrical rooms, UPS/battery rooms and mechanical plant (grey space) sit beside or below the halls.
  5. Meet-me rooms connect carriers; the NOC watches everything; generators and chillers sit outside or on the roof.

Who uses it

Facilities technicians, security officers, network engineers and site managers move through all these spaces daily; designers lay them out.

Key takeaway

Learn the TIA-942 cabling spaces in order from outside in: Entrance Room, Main Distribution Area, Horizontal Distribution Area, Equipment Distribution Area.

Going deeper

  • Sites are planned as security layers: perimeter fence and vehicle barriers, guarded gate, building entrance with mantrap, then hall and cage access, each needing separate authorisation.
  • A-side and B-side electrical rooms are often separated by fire-rated walls so one fire cannot take out both power paths, the idea behind Tier IV compartmentalisation.
  • TIA-942 names the telecom spaces from outside in: entrance room, main distribution area, horizontal distribution areas, optional zone distribution areas and equipment distribution areas at the racks.
  • Many modern AI halls sit on a concrete slab with overhead busway, cable trays and liquid-cooling pipework, because heavy racks and large pipes suit a solid floor better than raised tiles.
  • Support spaces such as spares stores, workshops, customer work areas and shipping rooms keep cardboard, dust and tools out of the halls, protecting air quality and limiting fire load.
  • Floor loading is specified early: dense AI racks and lithium battery cabinets weigh far more than older equipment and may need reinforced slabs or load-spreading plates.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Bringing cardboard into a data hall: it sheds fibres and dust that clog filters and adds fire load; unbox in the build room.
  • Assuming white space is the whole building: grey space, plant yards and support rooms often equal or exceed the IT floor area.
  • Treating the meet-me room as open to all staff: it is a high-security space entered only with approved access.

A pre-filled 1,400 kg AI rack rolls straight off the lorry onto the dock leveller. The second door opens only after the first closes and the visitor's badge and fingerprint both match. Ten 3 MW generators with belly tanks hold enough fuel for 48 hours at full load. Raised floor vs slab floorDesign choice · Concept · Current · Facilities Older halls use raised tiles to carry cold air and cables; many modern halls use a concrete slab with overhead cabling. A 2005 hall has a 600 mm raised floor; the new AI hall puts racks straight on the slab.

docs.title: 1.4 How a Data Centre Works: Power, Cooling and Network Paths
docs.text:
Every data centre runs three paths at the same time. The power path brings electricity from the grid down to each server, with batteries and generators as backup. The cooling path carries the heat away, and the network path carries data in and out over fibre-optic cables.

The power path, from grid to chip. Each stage loses a little energy, and almost all the power ends up as heat in the hall.

Think of it like…

It is like the human body: the power path is the blood supply, the cooling path is sweating and breathing out heat, and the network path is the nervous system carrying messages.

Real-world example

At a fictional 6 MW site, grid power arrives at 33,000 volts, is stepped down to 400 volts, and passes through UPS units to the racks. Each server takes power through two separate supplies, A and B. Cold air at 24 °C enters the server fronts, leaves the back at about 36 °C, and cooling units carry that heat via water to roof-top coolers. Meanwhile data arrives through two fibre routes into the meet-me room and flows over switches to the servers.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Power: grid → substation/transformer → switchgear → UPS → PDU → rack PDU → server power supplies.
  2. Backup: if the grid fails, batteries carry the load for minutes while generators start in seconds.
  3. Cooling: cool air or liquid takes heat from IT → cooling units → water loops → chillers or dry coolers → outside air.
  4. Network: carrier fibre → entrance room/MMR → border routers → spine and leaf switches → servers.
  5. Monitoring: BMS, EPMS and DCIM software watch every path and raise alarms.

Who uses it

Critical facilities engineers own power and cooling; network engineers own the network path; NOC operators watch all three.

Key takeaway

Almost all electricity used by IT ends up as heat, so cooling capacity must match power capacity: a 1 MW IT load needs roughly 1 MW of heat removal.

Going deeper

  • Losses add up along the chain: transformers, UPS conversion, cables and server power supplies each lose a few percent, which is why efficient UPS modes and higher distribution voltages matter at scale.
  • Standby generators typically start and accept load within about 10-15 seconds; UPS batteries or flywheels only bridge that gap, plus margin for a failed start and retry.
  • Air-cooled servers usually raise air temperature by around 10-15 °C; liquid-cooled racks move heat into water loops warm enough for dry coolers or heat reuse.
  • The network path is built like the power path, with at least two carriers on diverse routes, two meet-me rooms, and redundant border routers and spine switches.
  • BMS, EPMS and DCIM data feed the NOC; good sites correlate alarms across systems so a cooling fault and a rising rack temperature appear as one incident, not two.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking UPS batteries run the site for hours: they usually bridge only minutes until generators carry the load.
  • Planning power and cooling separately: adding IT power without matching cooling capacity creates hot spots and failures.
  • Assuming two power cords mean redundancy: they must connect to genuinely separate A and B paths, loaded so either can carry everything.

docs.title: Try it: Simple model: heat out equals power in (Python)

it_load_kw = 1000           # 1 MW of IT equipment
heat_kw = it_load_kw * 1.0  # nearly all becomes heat
btu_per_hr = heat_kw * 3412
tons = btu_per_hr / 12000
print(f"Heat to remove: {heat_kw:.0f} kW = {btu_per_hr:,.0f} BTU/h = {tons:.0f} tons of cooling")

docs.text: Name What it does Example Utility feed and substationGrid operator / utility · System · Current · Electrical The incoming connection from the public grid, often at medium or high voltage, sometimes with an on-site substation. docs.title: 1.5 Availability Maths and Redundancy: Nines, MTBF and N+1
docs.text:
Availability is the share of time a system is working, written as a percentage such as 99.99% ('four nines'). Data centres raise availability by adding spare equipment (redundancy) and by removing any single part whose failure would stop everything. A little maths tells you how much downtime each design allows and how much the spares really help.

Downtime allowed per year. Each extra nine cuts permitted downtime tenfold, and usually raises cost sharply.

Think of it like…

Redundancy is like carrying a spare tyre: one puncture no longer ends your journey, and carrying two spares (or a second car) protects you against even more bad luck, at a higher cost.

Real-world example

Leila, a junior engineer at the fictional Harbourview Data Centre, compares two cooling designs. Each chiller is available 99% of the time. With exactly the three chillers needed (N=3) in series logic, all three must work: 0.99³ ≈ 97.0%. Adding one spare (N+1, four chillers where any three suffice) raises cooling availability to about 99.94%, so the extra chiller is easy to justify.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Availability = uptime ÷ total time; turn it into minutes of downtime per year (525,600 minutes in a year).
  2. For a repairable part: Availability = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR).
  3. Parts in series (all needed): multiply their availabilities, so the chain is weaker than any one part.
  4. Parts in parallel (any one will do): 1 − (1 − A₁)(1 − A₂); redundancy multiplies the reliability.
  5. Find and remove single points of failure, then choose N, N+1, 2N or 2N+1 to match the business need and budget.

Who uses it

Design engineers, reliability engineers and site managers use these numbers to justify spending; cloud architects use the same maths for servers and zones.

Key takeaway

Memorise: 99.9% ≈ 8.8 hours a year, 99.99% ≈ 53 minutes, 99.999% ≈ 5.3 minutes of downtime.

Going deeper

  • Availability = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR), so cutting repair time helps as much as buying more reliable parts; on-site spares and trained staff shrink MTTR dramatically.
  • Reliability block diagrams model the path: series elements multiply availabilities, parallel redundant groups combine as one minus the product of unavailabilities, and the weakest series element dominates.
  • Redundancy only helps when failures are independent; common causes such as shared controls, contaminated fuel, firmware bugs or one person's error can disable 'redundant' units together.
  • Uptime Institute outage analyses consistently find human error and procedural failures involved in a large share of significant outages, so procedures and training matter as much as hardware.
  • Percentages hide frequency: one 53-minute outage and fifty one-minute blips both equal 99.99%, but the blips may crash far more servers and applications.
  • Cloud architects apply the same maths above the facility, spreading applications across zones so the application's availability exceeds that of any single building.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Adding availabilities instead of multiplying: two 99.9% parts in series give about 99.8%, not 99.9% or more.
  • Assuming N+1 everywhere removes all single points of failure: a shared breaker, busbar or control system can still drop everything.
  • Reading MTBF as life expectancy: 200,000 hours is an average failure rate across a population, not a promise one unit lasts 23 years.

MIN_PER_YEAR = 365 * 24 * 60   # 525,600
for a in (0.99, 0.999, 0.9999, 0.99999):
    print(f"{a*100:.3f}% -> {(1-a)*MIN_PER_YEAR:8.1f} min/year down")

# Availability from MTBF and MTTR (hours)

# Two identical units in parallel, either one is enough
a = 0.999

docs.title: 1.6 Tiers, Ratings and Availability Classes
docs.text:
Because 'reliable' means different things to different people, the industry uses a few classification systems that describe how resilient a data centre's power and cooling are. The best known is the Uptime Institute's Tier I to Tier IV. TIA-942 uses Rated-1 to Rated-4, and the European EN 50600 and international ISO/IEC 22237 standards use Availability Classes 1 to 4.

Uptime Institute Tier levels. Each Tier includes all the requirements of the Tiers below it.

Think of it like…

Tiers are like hotel star ratings for resilience: a one-star place gives you a bed, while a top-rated one has backup everything and can lose a generator mid-dinner without the lights flickering.

Real-world example

Coastline Insurance, a fictional firm, shortlists two colocation sites. Site A claims to be 'Tier III design' but holds no certificate; Site B holds Uptime Tier III Certification of Constructed Facility. Coastline's consultant explains that Tier III means any component can be maintained without switching off IT, but a single unplanned failure may still cause an outage. Coastline picks Site B and keeps a disaster-recovery copy in a second site 80 km away.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Tier I: basic capacity, a single path with no redundant components; maintenance means shutdown.
  2. Tier II: adds redundant capacity components (spare UPS modules, chillers) on a single distribution path.
  3. Tier III: concurrently maintainable; every component and path can be taken out for planned work without stopping IT.
  4. Tier IV: fault tolerant; the site survives any single unplanned failure, with compartmentalised, independent paths.
  5. Check whether a claim is self-declared or independently certified, and for which stage: design, constructed facility or operations.

Who uses it

Design engineers, consultants, colocation sales teams, auditors and customers' procurement teams use these classifications in every data centre deal.

Key takeaway

Concurrently maintainable (Tier III) protects against planned work; fault tolerant (Tier IV) also protects against an unplanned failure, yet neither promises zero downtime because people and procedures still matter.

Going deeper

  • Uptime certifies in stages: Tier Certification of Design Documents (TCDD), then Constructed Facility (TCCF) after on-site demonstrations, and separately Operational Sustainability (TCOS) for management and staffing.
  • Uptime's Tier Standard treats on-site engine generators as the primary power source and the utility as an economic alternative, so generators must be rated to run without runtime limits.
  • TIA-942 Rated-1 to Rated-4 and EN 50600 / ISO/IEC 22237 Availability Classes 1-4 follow similar logic, but each has its own rules, auditors and certificates, so the labels are not interchangeable.
  • The overall rating is set by the weakest subsystem: a 2N electrical design paired with single-path N+1 cooling cannot be Tier IV.
  • Tier IV adds compartmentalisation and continuous cooling: independent systems must be physically separated, and cooling must keep running through a power failure so dense racks do not overheat.
  • Most commercial colocation targets Tier III; Tier IV appears at some financial and government sites, while hyperscalers often achieve resilience in software across many sites instead.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Equating a Tier with an uptime percentage: the Tier Standard defines topology and behaviour, not guaranteed availability.
  • Accepting 'Tier III design' as proof: check whether the constructed facility and its operations are certified, and when.
  • Believing Tier IV means no outages: human error, poor maintenance or multiple failures can still cause downtime.

site = {"ups_units": 4, "ups_needed": 3, "power_paths": 2,
        "maintain_any_path_without_shutdown": True, "survives_any_single_fault": False}

spare = site["ups_units"] - site["ups_needed"]
print("UPS redundancy:", "N+%d" % spare if spare else "N (no spare)")

    print("Behaves like: fault tolerant (Tier IV / Class 4 concept)")
elif site["maintain_any_path_without_shutdown"] and site["power_paths"] >= 2:
    print("Behaves like: concurrently maintainable (Tier III / Class 3 concept)")

    print("Behaves like: basic capacity (Tier I / Class 1 concept)")

docs.title: 1.7 Key Metrics: PUE, WUE, CUE and Capacity
docs.text:
Data centres are measured by how much energy and water they use, how much carbon they emit and how well they use the capacity they built. The most famous number is PUE, which compares the energy for the whole building with the energy that actually reaches the IT equipment. A PUE of 1.0 would mean zero overhead; real sites range from about 1.1 to 2 or more.

PUE: from ideal to legacy. Lower is better; climate, design, load and measurement point all shift the number (middle and last bars are typical ranges).

Think of it like…

PUE is like a delivery company asking how much fuel the lorry burns compared with the weight of parcels it delivers: everything above the parcels themselves is overhead.

Real-world example

Over one year the fictional Northfield site uses 52,000 MWh in total, of which 40,000 MWh reaches IT equipment, so PUE = 52,000 ÷ 40,000 = 1.30. It also uses 72 million litres of water, giving WUE = 72,000,000 ÷ 40,000,000 kWh = 1.8 L/kWh. After adding hot-aisle containment and raising supply air temperature, next year's PUE falls to 1.22, saving about 3,200 MWh.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Meter total facility energy at the utility intake and IT energy at UPS outputs or rack PDUs.
  2. PUE = total facility energy ÷ IT equipment energy, measured over a full year to include all seasons.
  3. WUE = site water (litres) ÷ IT energy (kWh); CUE = CO₂ emissions (kg) ÷ IT energy (kWh).
  4. Track capacity: IT load in MW, kW per rack, utilisation and stranded capacity.
  5. Report and compare carefully; climate, design and measurement point all change the numbers.

Who uses it

Energy managers, sustainability teams, operations leaders and investors track these metrics; the EU now requires larger data centres to report them.

Key takeaway

PUE measures infrastructure overhead, not how useful the computing is: a site full of idle servers can still post a great PUE.

Going deeper

  • ISO/IEC 30134-2 defines PUE categories by where IT energy is metered: UPS output, PDU output or IT equipment input; later points are more accurate and give a higher, more honest PUE.
  • Design PUE is a calculated figure at planned load; operational PUE is measured over twelve months and is usually worse at low load, because fixed losses are spread over less IT energy.
  • WUE and PUE can trade against each other: evaporative cooling saves energy but consumes water, while air-cooled chillers save water but use more electricity, so read the metrics together.
  • CUE depends on grid carbon intensity; companies report location-based figures from local grids and market-based figures that credit purchased renewables, and the two can differ greatly.
  • The EU Energy Efficiency Directive requires data centres with at least 500 kW of installed IT power to report energy, water, renewable share and heat-reuse KPIs annually to a European database.
  • Capacity metrics drive revenue: sold versus built MW, utilisation and stranded capacity show how much more an operator can sell before new investment is needed.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing PUEs without context: a cool-climate hyperscaler and a tropical enterprise site cannot be judged on one number.
  • Quoting a single cool-night snapshot: standards require energy measured over a full year, including hot summers.
  • Thinking low PUE means efficient computing: PUE ignores how much useful work the servers actually do.

docs.title: 1.8 The Language of Power and Heat: Units for Beginners
docs.text:
Data centre people talk constantly in units of electricity and heat: watts, kilowatts, megawatts, volts, amps and kilowatt-hours. Power (watts) is how fast energy is used right now, while energy (kilowatt-hours) is how much was used over time. Heat is measured in the same watts, or in older units like BTU per hour and tons of refrigeration.

Power versus energy

Power (kW, MW) Energy (kWh, MWh) Measures How fast energy is used Total energy used Car analogy Speed Distance driven 15 kW rack 15 kW right now 131,400 kWh per year Used for Sizing cables, UPS, cooling Bills, PUE, carbon reports Heat link 1 kW ≈ 3,412 BTU/h 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ

Power is a rate; energy is power multiplied by time.

Think of it like…

Think of water from a tap: voltage is the pressure, current (amps) is the flow, power (watts) is how hard the water is working right now, and energy (kWh) is the total water that filled the bath.

Real-world example

Technician Dev checks a rack fed by a three-phase 400 V, 32 A circuit. Its capacity is √3 × 400 × 32 ≈ 22.2 kVA, or about 21 kW at a power factor of 0.95. The rack actually draws 15 kW, which over a year is 15 × 8,760 ≈ 131,400 kWh. That 15 kW also becomes about 51,000 BTU/h of heat, or roughly 4.3 tons of cooling.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Power (W) = volts (V) × amps (A) for simple DC or single-phase loads with power factor 1.
  2. Three-phase power ≈ √3 × line voltage × current × power factor.
  3. Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × hours; bills and PUE use energy, not power.
  4. Apparent power (kVA) × power factor = real power (kW); equipment is often rated in both.
  5. Heat: 1 kW ≈ 3,412 BTU/h; 1 ton of refrigeration = 12,000 BTU/h ≈ 3.517 kW.

Who uses it

Every technician, engineer, salesperson and planner uses these units daily; the power and cooling chapters build on them.

Key takeaway

Never mix up kW (power, a rate) and kWh (energy, an amount): '5 MW' describes size, '40,000 MWh' describes a year's use.

Going deeper

  • Conversions to memorise: 1 kW ≈ 3,412 BTU/h; 1 ton of refrigeration = 12,000 BTU/h ≈ 3.517 kW; 1 kWh = 3.6 megajoules; a year has 8,760 hours (8,784 in a leap year).
  • Transformers, UPS units and generators are rated in kVA because their heating depends on current, while IT loads and cooling plant are planned in kW.
  • Three-phase power is √3 (about 1.73) × line voltage × current × PF; at the same current, a 400 V three-phase feed carries about three times a 230 V single-phase feed.
  • Colocation is often priced per kW of committed power per month plus metered energy in kWh, so customers must understand both the rate and the amount.
  • Heat and airflow are linked: removing 1 kW with a 10 °C air temperature rise needs roughly 0.08 m³/s (about 175 CFM) of air.
  • Nameplate ratings overstate typical draw for ordinary servers, so planners use measured peaks; AI servers running training jobs operate much closer to their rated power.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing up kW and kWh: '10 MW' describes capacity; a year at full load is about 87,600 MWh.
  • Treating kVA and kW as equal: they match only at power factor 1.0, so check which one a datasheet quotes.
  • Forgetting √3 in three-phase sums, which underestimates circuit capacity by about 42%.

V, A, pf = 400, 32, 0.95        # 3-phase line voltage, amps, power factor
kva = math.sqrt(3) * V * A / 1000
kw = kva * pf
print(f"Circuit: {kva:.1f} kVA = {kw:.1f} kW at PF {pf}")
# Safe continuous loading is often limited to 80% of breaker rating
print(f"Planning limit at 80%: {kw*0.8:.1f} kW")

rack_kw = 15
print(f"Heat: {rack_kw*3412:,.0f} BTU/h = {rack_kw*3412/12000:.1f} tons")

Power factor (0-1) links them: kW = kVA × PF. A 500 kVA UPS with a 0.9 PF rating supports up to 450 kW of IT load. A 5 kW server rack gives off about 17,000 BTU/h. Ton of refrigeration (TR)Cooling capacity unit, mainly US · Concept · Current · Mechanical Cooling capacity of 12,000 BTU/h, about 3.517 kW, from the ice-melting origins of air conditioning. A 1,000-ton chiller removes about 3.5 MW of heat. Temperature and delta-T (ΔT)Thermodynamics · Concept · Current · Mechanical Delta-T is the temperature rise across equipment; more heat per litre or cubic metre moved means bigger ΔT. Air enters a server at 24 °C and leaves at 36 °C: a ΔT of 12 °C (12 K). Nameplate vs measured powerCapacity planning practice · Concept · Current · Operations Nameplate is the maximum a power supply is rated for; real draw is usually much lower, so planners measure actual use. A server labelled 1,600 W typically draws 600 W, so budgeting by nameplate strands capacity. Rack unit (U)EIA-310 / IEC 60297 · Concept · Current · Facilities The standard height slot in a rack: 1U = 1.75 inches (44.45 mm). A 2U server takes two slots; a 42U rack holds 21 of them before counting switches.

docs.title: 1.9 Site Selection: Where to Build a Data Centre
docs.text:
Choosing where to build a data centre is one of the biggest decisions in its life, because you cannot move a building later. The top questions are: can we get enough electricity soon enough, are there good fibre connections, and is the land safe from floods, earthquakes and storms? Cost, water, climate, skilled workers, laws and the local community's views all matter too.

Screening a site. Power and connectivity knock out most candidate plots before land price is discussed.

Think of it like…

Picking a data centre site is like choosing where to open a big bakery: you need a strong power supply for the ovens, good roads for deliveries, no flood risk, staff who live nearby and neighbours who will not complain about the noise at 4 a.m.

Real-world example

Solace Cloud, a fictional provider, compares three plots for a 60 MW campus. Plot A is next to a city but the utility cannot supply power until 2032. Plot B has power by 2028 but sits partly in a 1-in-100-year floodplain. Plot C, 70 km from the city, has a substation upgrade due in 2027, two fibre routes and cool winters for free cooling; at 70 km the extra round-trip delay is only about 0.7 ms, so Plot C wins.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Confirm power: grid capacity, connection date, cost and the option of on-site generation.
  2. Confirm connectivity: at least two diverse fibre routes and acceptable latency to users and other sites.
  3. Screen hazards: floodplains, earthquakes, hurricanes, wildfire, flight paths and nearby industrial risks.
  4. Check land, zoning, planning rules, water supply, tax incentives, climate and local workforce.
  5. Engage the community and regulators early about noise, water, diesel generators and jobs.

Who uses it

Site-selection consultants, real-estate and development teams, utility engineers and planning specialists do this work, often years before construction.

Key takeaway

Today the first question in most markets is 'how soon can we get power?': in many regions the grid connection, not land, decides where data centres go.

Going deeper

  • Developers often secure land with option agreements and pay for utility studies before buying, because a plot without a firm power date has little value for a data centre.
  • Latency rule of thumb: light in fibre covers about 200 km per millisecond, so each 100 km of route adds roughly 1 ms of round-trip delay before equipment delays.
  • Hazard screening uses flood maps (1-in-100 and 1-in-500-year zones), seismic maps, storm and wildfire records, flight paths and nearby hazardous industry or pipelines.
  • Disaster-recovery pairs and availability zones need separation: far enough apart to avoid shared disasters, close enough for synchronous replication, often tens of kilometres.
  • Power price and grid carbon intensity shape decades of operating cost; Nordic countries attract builders with cheap renewable power and cold climates despite distance from big cities.
  • Local opposition can stop projects: generator and fan noise, water use, diesel emissions, traffic and loss of farmland are common objections best addressed early.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Choosing land first and asking about power later: grid connection dates now decide feasibility in most major markets.
  • Assuming sites must be in the city: most applications tolerate a few milliseconds, so locations 50-100 km away often work.
  • Using straight-line distance for latency: real fibre routes can be much longer, so obtain route maps or measure.

docs.title: Try it: Fibre latency calculator: how far is too far? (Python)
docs.text:
# Light in glass fibre travels at roughly 200,000 km/s
# so about 5 microseconds per km one way.
for km in (10, 70, 100, 500, 2000):
    rtt_ms = km * 2 * 5 / 1000      # there and back, in milliseconds
    print(f"{km:5} km of fibre -> ~{rtt_ms:.1f} ms round trip (before equipment delays)")
# Real routes are longer than the straight line, so add a margin.

docs.title: 1.10 The Data Centre Lifecycle: Plan, Design, Build, Operate, Retire
docs.text:
A data centre goes through a long life: someone plans why it is needed, engineers design it, contractors build it, testers prove it works, operators run it for decades, and eventually it is upgraded or shut down. Each stage has its own documents, teams and risks. The building usually lasts 20 years or more, while the servers inside are replaced every few years.

The data centre lifecycle. The building lasts decades while the IT inside is refreshed every few years.

Think of it like…

It is like the life of a passenger aircraft: designed and certified, built, test-flown, flown daily with strict maintenance for decades, refitted with new seats and screens, and finally retired and recycled.

Real-world example

Meridian Health, a fictional hospital group, decides in 2025 it needs 4 MW for imaging and records. The business case and site search take 9 months, design 8 months and construction 16 months, using a design-build contractor. Commissioning runs through Levels 1 to 5, ending with a full integrated systems test with load banks before go-live in late 2027. Servers will be refreshed about every five years, while the UPS and chillers are planned to last 15-20 years.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Plan: business case, capacity forecast, budget, site selection and the owner's project requirements.
  2. Design: basis of design, then concept, schematic and detailed design with drawings and specifications.
  3. Build: procure equipment (often with long lead times), construct, install and inspect.
  4. Commission: test from factory (Level 1) to integrated systems test (Level 5), then hand over.
  5. Operate, refresh and expand; finally decommission, sanitise data and recycle equipment.

Who uses it

Developers, project managers, architects, MEP engineers, contractors, commissioning agents, operators and IT asset disposal firms each own a stage.

Key takeaway

Long-lead items such as transformers, switchgear and generators can take a year or more to arrive, so they are often ordered before the design is finished.

Going deeper

  • Commissioning levels: L1 factory witness tests, L2 delivery and installation checks, L3 start-up, L4 functional performance tests, and L5 integrated systems test with load banks and simulated failures.
  • Long-lead items in the 2020s included large power transformers, MV switchgear, generators and chillers; owners often reserve manufacturing slots or pre-order before design is complete.
  • Hyperscalers standardise designs and repeat them across many sites, compressing schedules; developers deliver powered shells or full fit-outs under long build-to-suit leases.
  • Electrical and mechanical plant typically lasts 15-25 years while servers are replaced every 3-6 years, so halls are often retrofitted mid-life for higher density or liquid cooling.
  • Handover packages include as-built drawings, O&M manuals, test records, warranties, training and spares; weak handover documentation is a frequent root cause of later operational errors.
  • Decommissioning follows media-sanitisation guidance such as NIST SP 800-88 with certificates of destruction, plus electronics recycling rules such as the EU WEEE Directive.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Rushing Level 5 testing to hit a go-live date: problems then surface during real outages with customer load.
  • Designing only for day-one load: plan for density growth, phased expansion and future liquid cooling from the start.
  • Treating decommissioning as unplugging: data must be sanitised and documented, and equipment disposed of legally.

docs.title: Try it: Rough project timeline and go-live date (Python)
docs.text:
from datetime import date, timedelta
phases = [("Business case & site", 9), ("Design", 8), ("Construction", 16), ("Commissioning", 3)]
start = date(2025, 1, 1)
for name, months in phases:
    end = start + timedelta(days=round(months * 30.4))
    print(f"{name:22} {start} -> {end}")
    start = end
print("Planned go-live:", start)

docs.title: 1.11 Who Works in a Data Centre?
docs.text:
A data centre looks quiet, but many people keep it running: technicians on 24/7 shifts, electrical and mechanical engineers, network specialists, security officers and managers. Behind them are designers, builders, commissioning experts, sales teams and sustainability specialists. Many careers start as an entry-level technician and grow from there.

The team behind the site. Most careers start on the shift team and specialise from there.

Think of it like…

A data centre team is like an airport: few passengers see the engineers, controllers, security staff and ground crew, but every flight depends on all of them doing their part.

Real-world example

At the fictional Eastgate campus, a night shift has two critical-facilities technicians, one data centre technician, one NOC operator and two security officers. At 02:00 a customer requests remote hands to reseat a server; the data centre technician does it in 15 minutes. At 04:30 a cooling unit alarms, and the mechanical technician swaps a failed fan using the approved procedure while the NOC operator updates the customer.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Operations teams run the site 24/7 on shifts: technicians, engineers and NOC staff.
  2. Security officers control access, patrol and monitor cameras.
  3. IT and network staff install and maintain servers, cabling and switches.
  4. Project, design, construction and commissioning teams build new capacity.
  5. Business teams sell space, manage customers and report on sustainability and safety.

Who uses it

This section is for anyone considering a data centre career; the careers chapter covers qualifications and progression in depth.

Key takeaway

Employers value a safety mindset, the habit of following written procedures exactly, and calm communication as much as technical knowledge.

Going deeper

  • Operations usually runs 24/7 on rotating shifts, such as 12-hour days and nights, backed by on-call senior engineers and vendor field engineers for specialist repairs.
  • Critical facilities roles often recruit from trades such as electricians and HVAC technicians, and from military or marine engineering, whose plant experience transfers well.
  • Work follows written procedures: SOPs for routine tasks, MOPs for specific changes and EOPs for emergencies, approved through change management before anyone touches live systems.
  • Entry routes include IT support, electrical or mechanical apprenticeships, military service and vendor or industry training; the careers chapter covers certifications and progression.
  • Soft skills matter: clear shift handovers, accurate logs, calm escalation and good customer communication prevent many incidents and are tested in interviews.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming it is all IT work: much of the job is operating and maintaining electrical and mechanical plant.
  • Improvising during an incident: technicians follow approved EOPs and escalate rather than guessing on live systems.
  • Dismissing safety training as paperwork: arc-flash and lockout rules protect your life from day one.
