docs.title: 1.12 Follow a Request: From Your Phone to a Server and Back
docs.text:
When you tap an app, your request travels across the internet into a data centre, through its network to a server, which may fetch data from storage, and the answer returns the same way, usually in well under a second. Every step depends on the data centre's power and cooling working perfectly. Following one request is the best way to see how all the pieces fit together.

One app request, end to end. The whole trip usually takes well under a second, crossing several networks and buildings.

Think of it like…

It is like posting a letter that asks a question: it goes to the local sorting office, travels on motorways, arrives at a guarded office building, is passed desk to desk to the right expert, who checks the files and sends a reply back.

Real-world example

Zara opens the fictional TrailMap app. Her phone asks DNS for the address, and a nearby CDN server returns the map images in 15 ms. The request for her saved routes travels via her mobile operator and an internet exchange into a colocation site, through the meet-me room, a firewall and a load balancer, then over leaf and spine switches to an application server. The server reads her routes from a database on flash storage and replies; the whole trip takes about 120 ms.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. DNS turns the app's domain name into an IP address, often pointing to a nearby CDN or edge site.
  2. Traffic crosses the mobile or broadband network and an internet exchange or transit provider.
  3. It enters the data centre over carrier fibre to the meet-me room and the operator's border routers.
  4. Firewalls and load balancers check and spread requests; spine and leaf switches carry them to a server.
  5. The server reads or writes storage and replies the same way, with UPS, generators and cooling keeping every device alive.

Who uses it

Network, cloud and site reliability engineers trace requests like this when troubleshooting; facilities teams keep the physical path powered and cooled.

Key takeaway

When asked 'what happens when you open a website?', mention both the logical path (DNS, TCP/TLS, HTTP) and the physical path (fibre, MMR, switches, servers, power and cooling).

Going deeper

  • DNS answers can be steered by geography: providers return the address of the nearest healthy edge site or region, so users in different countries reach different data centres.
  • TLS 1.3 needs one round trip to agree keys (zero with session resumption), so distance to the server directly affects how quickly secure pages start loading.
  • Inside the data centre, east-west traffic between servers often exceeds north-south traffic to users; one request may trigger dozens of internal calls to microservices and databases.
  • Leaf-spine fabrics keep every server pair the same number of hops apart and use ECMP routing to spread traffic across all spine switches.
  • The physical path is redundant end to end: dual carriers on diverse routes, two meet-me rooms, paired routers and firewalls, and servers on separate A and B power.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming one data centre serves everything: CDNs, edge caches and several regions often serve parts of a single page.
  • Forgetting the physical layer when troubleshooting: a failed optic or cross-connect causes 'network' problems no software change will fix.
  • Equating bandwidth with latency: a faster link carries more data, but distance still sets the minimum delay.

docs.title: Try it: Trace and time a request from your own machine
docs.text:
nslookup example.com                 # DNS lookup (Windows, macOS, Linux)
tracert example.com                  # Windows: list the routers on the path
traceroute example.com               # macOS / Linux
curl -o /dev/null -s -w "dns=%{time_namelookup}s connect=%{time_connect}s tls=%{time_appconnect}s total=%{time_total}s\n" https://example.com

Zara's phone asks a resolver for trailmap.example and gets an address in 20 ms. Map images load from a CDN server in the same city instead of a distant data centre. The mobile operator and the app's hosting provider exchange traffic at an IXP rather than via a third party. Zara's saved routes are read from an NVMe flash array in under a millisecond. The padlock in the browser shows a TLS connection to the site. docs.title: 1.13 The AI Data Centre Boom in Brief
docs.text:
Artificial intelligence, especially large language models, runs on graphics processors (GPUs) and other accelerators that use far more power and produce far more heat than ordinary servers. That has pushed rack power from around 10 kW to over 100 kW, made liquid cooling mainstream, and turned access to electricity into the biggest limit on growth. Companies are now planning campuses measured in gigawatts.

Why AI reshapes data centres. Each link in the chain explains a trend you will meet in the industry.

Think of it like…

Ordinary servers are like family cars; AI racks are like Formula 1 cars, packing enormous power into a small space and needing a specialised pit crew, fuel supply and cooling to keep them running.

Real-world example

The fictional company Lumen AI wants a 20 MW training cluster. Its old colocation halls were designed for 8 kW racks with air cooling, so the new cluster of liquid-cooled racks at about 130 kW each needs a purpose-built hall with coolant distribution units and heavier floors. Just 150 such racks fill the 20 MW budget, compared with 2,500 traditional racks. The hardest part is securing grid power by the date the GPUs arrive.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Training builds a model by running huge clusters of GPUs flat out for weeks; inference answers user requests afterwards.
  2. GPUs are packed densely and linked by very fast networks, so racks draw 100 kW or more.
  3. Air cannot remove that much heat, so direct-to-chip liquid cooling becomes the norm.
  4. Grid connections become the bottleneck, driving on-site generation, nuclear deals and new locations.
  5. Campuses grow to hundreds of megawatts or gigawatts, changing how the whole industry designs and builds.

Who uses it

Hyperscalers, AI labs, GPU cloud providers, colocation developers, utilities and governments are all reshaping plans around AI demand.

Key takeaway

Remember the chain: AI models → GPUs → very high rack power → liquid cooling → huge grid demand; each link explains a trend you will be asked about.

Going deeper

  • Accelerator power climbs with each generation: NVIDIA's A100 SXM was rated around 400 W, the H100 SXM up to 700 W, and Blackwell-generation GPUs around 1,000 W or more.
  • Training clusters must sit close together on very fast networks, so a single AI cluster can need tens to hundreds of megawatts in one building or campus.
  • Inference is spread across more locations and is expected to become a growing share of AI demand as people and businesses use AI services every day.
  • Rack-scale systems such as NVIDIA's NVL72 move design decisions from the server to the whole rack: power shelves, busbars, coolant manifolds and network switches arrive pre-integrated.
  • The IEA's 2025 Energy and AI report projected global data-centre electricity use roughly doubling to about 945 TWh by 2030, with AI the main driver.
  • Supply chains tightened for GPUs, high-bandwidth memory, transformers, switchgear, generators and skilled electricians, so equipment delivery often decides when capacity goes live.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming old halls can host AI racks with minor changes: power distribution, cooling and floor loading usually need major retrofits.
  • Thinking AI demand is only training: inference runs continuously and is expected to become a major share of load.
  • Treating gigawatt announcements as built capacity: most are phased plans that depend on power, permits and financing.

docs.text:
gpus_per_rack = 72
watts_per_gpu = 1200          # illustrative accelerator power
overhead = 1.5                # CPUs, memory, network, fans, power losses (rough)
rack_kw = gpus_per_rack * watts_per_gpu * overhead / 1000
racks = 150
pue = 1.2
print(f"Per rack: ~{rack_kw:.0f} kW")
print(f"IT load: ~{rack_kw*racks/1000:.1f} MW")
print(f"From the grid (PUE {pue}): ~{rack_kw*racks*pue/1000:.1f} MW")

docs.title: Glossary of Terms
A
docs.text: Adiabatic cooling Cooling air by evaporating water into it, using far less energy than mechanical refrigeration. Arc flash A dangerous explosive release of energy when electricity jumps through air between conductors. ASHRAE The American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers; its TC 9.9 committee publishes data-centre thermal guidelines. ATS Automatic Transfer Switch — moves an electrical load from the utility supply to a generator (and back) automatically.

docs.title: B
docs.text: BESS Battery Energy Storage System — large battery installation that stores energy for backup or grid services. BMS Building Management System — software and controllers that monitor and control mechanical plant such as chillers and air handlers. Business continuity Keeping critical services running through disruption, using plans, alternative sites and tested recovery procedures. Busway An overhead enclosed metal bar system that distributes power along a row; racks tap into it with plug-in units.

docs.title: C
docs.text: CDU Coolant Distribution Unit — pumps and controls the liquid loop that feeds direct-to-chip cold plates, with a heat exchanger to facility water. Chiller A machine that removes heat from water using a refrigeration cycle, producing chilled water for cooling. Cold aisle The aisle where server fronts face each other and draw in cool air. Colocation Renting space, power and cooling in a data centre owned by a provider, while you own the IT equipment. Commissioning The structured testing (Levels 1-5) that proves a facility's systems work as designed before going live. Concurrent maintainability Every component can be taken out for planned maintenance without shutting down IT; the key Tier III requirement. CRAC / CRAH Computer Room Air Conditioner (has its own compressor) / Computer Room Air Handler (uses chilled water). Critical path The longest chain of dependent tasks in a project schedule; any delay on it delays the finish date. Cross-connect A physical cable connecting two customers or a customer and a carrier inside a data centre. CUE Carbon Usage Effectiveness — total CO2 emissions from data-centre energy divided by IT energy.

docs.title: D
docs.text: DCIM Data Centre Infrastructure Management — software that tracks assets, power, cooling and capacity in one view. Delta-T The temperature difference between incoming and outgoing air or water; higher delta-T usually means more efficient cooling. Direct-to-chip cooling Liquid cooling where coolant flows through cold plates mounted directly on CPUs and GPUs. Disaster recovery (DR) Restoring IT systems and data at another site after a serious failure such as fire, flood or cyber attack.

docs.title: E
docs.text: Economiser Equipment that uses cool outside air or water to cool the data centre without running compressors (free cooling). Edge data centre A small facility placed close to users or devices to reduce latency. EPMS Electrical Power Monitoring System — monitors meters, breakers and power quality across the electrical system.

docs.title: F
docs.text: Fault tolerance The ability to keep IT running through any single unplanned failure; the key Tier IV requirement.

docs.title: G
docs.text: Generator An engine-driven machine (usually diesel) that produces electricity when the utility supply fails. GMP (Guaranteed maximum price) A construction contract ceiling price; the contractor pays overruns unless the owner changes the scope. Grey space Back-of-house areas holding electrical and mechanical plant such as UPS, switchgear and chillers.

docs.title: H
docs.text: Hot aisle The aisle where server backs face each other and exhaust hot air. Hyperscale Very large data centres or campuses run by cloud and internet giants, often hundreds of megawatts.

docs.title: I
docs.text: Immersion cooling Submerging servers in a non-conductive fluid that absorbs heat directly (single-phase or two-phase). IST Integrated Systems Test — Level 5 commissioning, testing all systems together under simulated real conditions.

docs.title: K
docs.text: kW per rack Power drawn by one rack; a key measure of density (about 5-15 kW for traditional IT, 100 kW+ for AI racks).

docs.title: L
docs.text: LOTO Lockout/Tagout — locking and labelling energy sources so equipment cannot be re-energised during work.

docs.title: M
docs.text: Meet-me room (MMR) A secure room where carriers and customers interconnect their networks. MOP Method of Procedure — a step-by-step approved plan for a specific maintenance or change task. MW (megawatt) One million watts; data-centre capacity is usually quoted in MW of IT load.

docs.title: N
docs.text: N, N+1, 2N Redundancy levels: N = just enough, N+1 = one spare, 2N = a full duplicate system. NOC Network/Operations Centre — the room where staff monitor the facility and network 24/7.

docs.title: O
docs.text: OCP Open Compute Project — a community sharing open hardware designs for servers, racks and data centres. Operational technology (OT) The control systems, such as BMS, EPMS, PLCs and equipment controllers, that run physical plant like power and cooling.

docs.title: P
docs.text: PDU Power Distribution Unit — distributes power to racks; a rack PDU is the power strip inside a rack. PPA Power Purchase Agreement — a long-term contract to buy electricity, often from a new wind or solar farm. Pre-action sprinkler A sprinkler system whose pipes stay dry until a detector confirms fire, reducing accidental water damage. PUE Power Usage Effectiveness — total facility energy divided by IT equipment energy; 1.0 is the theoretical ideal.

docs.title: R
docs.text: Rack A standard metal frame (usually 19 inches wide) that holds servers and network gear, measured in rack units (U). Rack unit (U) The standard height unit in a rack: 1U = 1.75 inches (44.45 mm). Raised floor A floor of removable tiles on pedestals, creating a void for cables or cool air. Rear-door heat exchanger A water-cooled coil fitted to the back door of a rack that removes heat as air leaves the servers. Redundancy Extra components or paths so one failure does not stop the service. Remote hands A colocation service where on-site staff perform simple tasks on a customer's equipment. RPO / RTO Recovery Point Objective (how much data you can lose) and Recovery Time Objective (how long you can be down). RPP Remote Power Panel — a cabinet of breakers near the racks, fed from a PDU, that supplies individual rack circuits.

docs.title: S
docs.text: SCADA Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition — industrial control software used to monitor and operate electrical and mechanical plant. SLA Service Level Agreement — a contract promising availability, power or response times, with penalties if missed. Spine-leaf A two-layer data-centre network where every leaf switch connects to every spine switch. STS Static Transfer Switch — switches a load between two power sources electronically in a few milliseconds. Switchgear Assemblies of breakers and switches that control, protect and isolate electrical circuits.

docs.title: T
docs.text: TCO (Total cost of ownership) All costs of buying, running and financing an asset over its life, used to compare build, lease and cloud options. TIA-942 The Telecommunications Industry Association standard for data-centre infrastructure, with Rated-1 to Rated-4 levels. Tier Uptime Institute's four-level classification (I-IV) of data-centre infrastructure resilience. Transformer Equipment that changes voltage, e.g. stepping medium voltage down to low voltage for the building. Triple-net (NNN) lease A lease where the tenant pays rent plus operating costs such as power, taxes, insurance and maintenance.

docs.title: U
docs.text: UPS Uninterruptible Power Supply — batteries and electronics that keep IT running instantly when power fails. Uptime / nines Availability expressed as a percentage, e.g. 99.99% ('four nines') is about 53 minutes of downtime per year.

docs.title: V
docs.text: VESDA Very Early Smoke Detection Apparatus — an aspirating system that samples air to detect smoke very early.

docs.title: W
docs.text: White space The room where IT racks live, also called the data hall or computer room. WUE Water Usage Effectiveness — litres of site water used per kWh of IT energy.

docs.title: How to read this guide
docs.text: Each topic follows the same simple pattern, so you can jump to any page and understand it without reading the rest first.

docs.title: How each topic is built
docs.text:
In plain English A jargon-free explanation of what the topic is. Think of it like… An everyday analogy that makes the idea click. Real-world example A short realistic story or worked example showing it in action. How it works The key steps, in order. Who uses it The people, jobs and industries that rely on it. Key takeaway The single most important thing to remember.

Many topics include a Try it box with a safe command or snippet. Then a table lists the most important entries — with what each one does and a concrete example.

docs.title: Entry type labels
docs.text:
Concept, Metric, Standard, Regulation, Equipment, Component, System, Technology, Facility, Material, Practice, Procedure, Document, Tool, Software, Product, Service, Company, Organisation, Certification, Role, Resource, Market, Incident

Concept = an idea to understand. Equipment / Component / System = physical plant. Standard / Regulation = an official rule or specification. Metric = something you measure. Tool / Software = something you use. Company / Organisation = who builds, owns or sets the rules. Incident = a real outage worth learning from.

docs.title: Status labels
docs.text:
Current, Legacy, Emerging

Current = widely used in data centres today. Legacy = still found in older sites but being replaced or phased out. Emerging = new and being adopted, especially for AI-era facilities.

docs.title: Discipline labels
docs.text:
Electrical, Mechanical, Facilities, Security, It, Operations, Sustainability, Business, General

Shows which team usually owns the topic: Electrical (power), Mechanical (cooling), Facilities (building, racks, fire), Security (physical protection), IT (servers, storage, network), Operations, Sustainability, or Business (commercial, market, careers).

docs.title: About this guide
docs.text: This guide is for students and self-learners. Standard numbers, tier definitions, metrics, company ownership and market facts were checked for accuracy as of late 2026, but this industry moves fast — deals close, regulations change and new AI campuses are announced every month. Always check the Uptime Institute, TIA, CENELEC/ISO, ASHRAE, the EU and company filings for the latest. Product and company names belong to their owners; all people and organisations in the examples are fictional.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Industry, Players, Careers & Learning
docs.text: This chapter steps back from the equipment to look at the industry itself: how data centres make money, what they cost to build, run and finance, who the big builders, landlords and suppliers are, and where in the world the action is. It then turns to you, setting out the jobs available, the certifications employers recognise, the best free resources and how to answer common interview questions. Company facts were checked as of late 2026, but ownership and deals change fast, so always verify the latest before quoting them.

docs.title: 8.1 How the Data Centre Industry Makes Money
docs.text:
Data centres are expensive buildings that someone has to pay for, so the industry has a few standard ways of doing business. Some giant tech companies build their own, while specialist landlords build and rent space, power and cooling to others. Rent is usually charged per kilowatt (kW) of power reserved each month, because power, not floor space, is the scarce thing.

Where the money flows. Signed leases are what turn investor money into buildings; power is usually passed through to tenants.

Think of it like…

It is like housing: some people build their own house, some rent a whole house built to their wishes, and some rent one flat in a big shared block with a concierge.

Real-world example

Fictional landlord Harbourline DC builds a 36 MW campus and pre-leases 24 MW to a cloud company on a 15-year contract at an illustrative $140 per kW per month. That one contract brings in about $40 million a year, which lets Harbourline borrow money to finish construction. The remaining 12 MW is sold as retail colocation to 60 smaller customers at higher prices per kW, plus monthly fees for cross-connects.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A developer secures land, planning permission and, most importantly, a grid connection.
  2. It signs anchor tenants before or during construction (pre-leasing) to de-risk the project.
  3. Banks, REIT shareholders or infrastructure funds finance the build against those signed leases.
  4. Customers pay monthly rent per kW reserved, plus power used, cross-connects and services.
  5. Mature, fully leased buildings are often sold or refinanced to investors to fund the next project.

Who uses it

Developers, investors, brokers, sales teams and hyperscaler real-estate teams live in this world; every engineer benefits from knowing why the money flows the way it does.

Key takeaway

In interviews remember that capacity is sold in kW or MW of critical IT load, and that low vacancy plus long lead times for power equipment are what drive prices up.

Going deeper

  • Wholesale deals are priced per kW of critical IT capacity per month, often with annual rent escalators of a few percent, while electricity is passed through at cost or with a margin.
  • Retail colocation earns more per kW, and interconnection is its highest-margin product: each cross-connect has a one-off installation charge (NRC) and a monthly recurring charge (MRC).
  • Development economics compare yield on cost with the yield buyers pay for stabilised assets; the gap is the developer's value creation, which is why leased buildings are often sold or recapitalised.
  • Tenant credit quality drives financing: a 15-year lease with an investment-grade hyperscaler can support large construction loans and, later, asset-backed securities.
  • Market reports track inventory (MW built), MW under construction, pre-leased share, net absorption, vacancy and asking rents, published regularly by major brokers.
  • Risks include customer concentration, equipment and grid delays, technology obsolescence as rack densities jump, and refinancing costs when interest rates rise.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Quoting capacity in square metres; the industry prices and plans in kW and MW of critical IT load.
  • Confusing contracted, built and energised megawatts; announcements often count capacity that is years from operation.
  • Assuming low vacancy guarantees profit; construction delays, power costs and tenant concentration can still hurt returns.

docs.title: Try it: Estimate yearly lease revenue for a building (illustrative prices only)
docs.text:
# Python: lease revenue = kW leased x price per kW per month x 12
leases = {
    'Cloud anchor (wholesale)': (24_000, 140),   # kW, $/kW/month (illustrative)
    'Retail colo customers':    (9_000, 260),
}
total = 0
for name, (kw, price) in leases.items():
    yearly = kw * price * 12
    total += yearly
    print(f'{name:28s} {kw/1000:5.1f} MW  ${yearly/1e6:6.1f}m per year')
print(f'Total: ${total/1e6:.1f}m per year')
print(f'Vacancy: {(36_000-33_000)/36_000:.0%} of a 36 MW building')

A fictional insurer sells its 4 MW site for cash and signs a 12-year lease to keep using it. docs.title: 8.2 Data Centre Costs, TCO & Financing
docs.text:
Data centres cost enormous sums to build and run. Building costs are usually counted per megawatt (MW) of IT capacity, running costs are dominated by electricity, and AI servers can cost more than the building around them. Total cost of ownership (TCO) adds everything up over the years, and financing explains where the money comes from: company cash, loans, investors and bonds.

How a wholesale data centre gets funded. Signed leases unlock cheaper money at each stage; vacancy or delay breaks the chain.

Think of it like…

It is like buying and running a car: the price matters, but fuel, insurance, servicing and loan interest over ten years can add up to more than the car itself.

Real-world example

Fictional developer Harbourline plans a 40 MW wholesale building. At an illustrative $13 million per MW the facility costs about $520 million before any IT, plus land and grid-connection charges. It signs a 15-year triple-net lease with a cloud company, so the tenant pays power, insurance and taxes on top of rent. Banks lend most of the build cost against that lease, and once the building is full Harbourline refinances with asset-backed bonds and recycles its equity into the next campus.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Estimate capital cost per MW for land, shell, power, cooling and fit-out, plus IT equipment if you are the user.
  2. Estimate yearly operating cost: electricity, staff, maintenance, insurance, taxes, water and connectivity.
  3. Combine them over the asset's life into TCO, using depreciation periods and a discount rate.
  4. Fund the build with equity, construction loans or joint ventures, usually backed by signed leases.
  5. Refinance stabilised buildings through long-term debt, securitisation or asset sales, and reinvest the capital.

Who uses it

Finance analysts, cost managers, development directors, investment and real-estate professionals, data-centre finance teams and the engineers who write business cases.

Key takeaway

Memorise the scale: North American greenfield facilities cost roughly $9-23 million per MW in 2026 before IT, and electricity is usually the biggest running cost.

Going deeper

  • Cost-per-MW figures vary hugely with location, redundancy, density and scope, so always check whether a number includes land, grid connection, fit-out and IT equipment.
  • Cushman & Wakefield found per-MW construction costs rose about 21% between late 2024 and its August 2026 guide, driven by equipment prices, labour wages and supply constraints.
  • For AI deployments the IT bill dominates: industry estimates put total spending for a gigawatt of AI capacity in the tens of billions of dollars, mostly accelerators and networking.
  • Lenders size loans using tenant credit, lease length and debt-service coverage; an investment-grade 15-year lease supports far more debt than short retail contracts.
  • Depreciation choices move reported profits by billions: a longer server life lowers yearly depreciation, which is why analysts debate how long AI GPUs stay economically useful.
  • Hidden costs include grid-connection contributions, rising insurance premiums, property-tax changes when incentives end and early refits when rack densities outgrow a building.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing cost-per-MW figures without checking scope; one may exclude land, grid works, fit-out or IT entirely.
  • Leaving electricity out of TCO; over ten years the power bill for a busy site can rival or exceed the cost of the building.
  • Assuming long leases remove all risk; tenant concentration, delays and rate rises can still sink an overleveraged developer.

docs.title: Try it: Ten-year TCO of 1 MW of IT load (Python, illustrative numbers)
docs.text:
mw, years = 1.0, 10
capex_per_mw = 13_000_000        # facility build, USD (illustrative)
pue, price_kwh = 1.3, 0.08       # efficiency and USD per kWh
staff_maint_per_year = 400_000   # illustrative

energy_kwh = mw * 1000 * 8760 * pue          # per year
energy_cost = energy_kwh * price_kwh
tco = capex_per_mw * mw + years * (energy_cost + staff_maint_per_year)
print(f"Yearly energy: {energy_kwh/1e6:.1f} GWh = ${energy_cost:,.0f}")
print(f"10-year TCO (no IT, no financing): ${tco:,.0f}")

Build vs lease vs cloudEnterprise and hyperscaler decision practice · Concept · Current · Business Choosing between owning a facility, renting colocation or using public cloud, trading control and long-run cost against speed and flexibility. A retailer moves steady workloads to colocation and keeps seasonal peaks in the cloud after a TCO study. Depreciation and useful lifeAccounting standards; company filings · Concept · Current · Business Spreading an asset's cost over its expected life: buildings over decades, servers over about five to six years at large cloud firms. In 2025 Meta lengthened many servers' lives to 5.5 years, while Amazon cut some from six to five years, citing AI's pace. Triple-net (NNN) leaseReal-estate lease structure · Concept · Current · Business Lease where the tenant pays rent plus operating costs such as power, taxes, insurance and maintenance; common for wholesale data centres. A hyperscaler on an NNN lease pays its own electricity and a share of property tax on top of rent. All-in colocation pricingRetail colocation contracts · Concept · Current · Business Retail contracts that bundle space, cooling and a power allowance into one monthly fee, or add metered power as a separate charge. A small firm pays one monthly fee per cabinet covering space, cooling and up to 6 kW of power. Construction loanBanks and private-credit lenders · Service · Current · Business Short-term loan funding a build in stages as work progresses, usually repaid by long-term debt once tenants occupy the building. Lenders release funds monthly after an independent monitor certifies the work completed. Data-centre securitisation (ABS and CMBS)Bond markets and rating agencies · Concept · Current · Business Bundling rents from leased data centres into rated bonds sold to investors, often cheaper long-term debt than bank loans. A developer issues asset-backed notes secured on five fully leased buildings and uses the cash to build more. Joint ventures and off-balance-sheet financinge.g. Meta and Blue Owl (Hyperion, 2025); Equinix xScale · Concept · Current · Business Investors own the buildings in a joint venture while the user leases them, sharing cost and keeping large debts off the user's balance sheet. In Meta's Hyperion deal, a venture majority-owned by Blue Owl funds the Louisiana campus and Meta signs as tenant. Cap rate and valuationReal-estate investors · Metric · Current · Business Capitalisation rate: yearly net operating income divided by property value; lower cap rates mean buyers pay more per dollar of rent. A stabilised campus earning $60m a year sells at a 6% cap rate, valuing it at $1bn. Cost of capitalCorporate finance · Concept · Current · Business Blended return demanded by lenders and shareholders; higher interest rates raise it and can make marginal projects unviable. When rates rise two points, Harbourline delays one building because its expected yield no longer beats its cost of capital.

docs.title: 8.3 Hyperscalers: The Biggest Builders
docs.text:
Hyperscalers are the handful of giant cloud and internet companies that run millions of servers and build data centres at enormous scale. They both build their own campuses and lease huge amounts of capacity from landlords. Since the AI boom, their yearly spending on buildings, power and chips has grown to hundreds of billions of dollars.

Two kinds of hyperscaler

Sell public cloud Build mainly for own services Examples AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, OCI, Alibaba Meta, ByteDance, Apple Revenue from Renting compute and services Ads, apps, devices, subscriptions Custom chips Trainium, Maia, TPU MTIA, Apple silicon Capacity mix Self-build, leases, neoclouds Self-build plus leases Who you meet Cloud customers and partners Internal product teams

Both build at enormous scale, but only cloud sellers rent capacity to the public.

Think of it like…

Hyperscalers are like the biggest supermarket chains: they own giant warehouses, also rent space from others, and their buying decisions shape the whole supply chain.

Real-world example

Fictional cloud firm Nimbus Corp plans a new AI region. It self-builds two 150 MW buildings on land it owns and leases another 100 MW from a developer to get capacity sooner. It orders transformers and chillers 30 months ahead and signs a long-term power deal for a new wind farm. Local colleges start training technicians because the campus will need about 300 staff.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Forecast demand for cloud and AI services years ahead.
  2. Choose regions based on power, fibre, land, tax, water and customers.
  3. Mix self-build campuses with leased wholesale capacity and neocloud contracts.
  4. Standardise designs so the same building can be copied quickly around the world.
  5. Report capital expenditure (capex) to investors every quarter, which the whole industry watches.

Who uses it

Thousands of engineers, technicians, construction managers and suppliers work for or with hyperscalers; many entry-level technician jobs are at their campuses.

Key takeaway

Know the difference between hyperscalers that sell cloud (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle, Alibaba) and those building mainly for their own apps (Meta, ByteDance, Apple).

Going deeper

  • Hyperscale campuses typically range from 100 MW to well over 1 GW, built from repeated standard building designs so equipment orders, construction and commissioning can be copied worldwide.
  • Hyperscalers mix self-build, wholesale leases and neocloud contracts: leasing buys speed, while self-build buys control and lower long-run cost.
  • Quarterly capex guidance is the industry's most-watched demand signal; suppliers of transformers, generators, chillers and GPUs move with these numbers.
  • Custom silicon such as TPU, Trainium, Maia and MTIA reduces dependence on one GPU vendor and lets operators design racks, power and cooling around their own chips.
  • Cloud architecture uses regions made of availability zones, each with independent power and cooling, so a hyperscaler's physical design follows its software resilience model.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling every large data-centre owner a hyperscaler; the term means companies operating at massive cloud or internet scale.
  • Assuming hyperscalers own all their capacity; they lease large amounts from developers and neoclouds.
  • Treating announced capex as already-built capacity; projects take years and can be delayed or cancelled.

docs.title: Try it: Rough sizing: how many GPUs fit in a given IT load (illustrative assumptions)
docs.text:
# Python: rough GPU count for a site (all inputs are assumptions)
it_load_mw = 150            # critical IT load
kw_per_gpu_all_in = 1.8     # GPU + CPU, network, storage share (assumed)
pue = 1.25

gpus = it_load_mw * 1000 / kw_per_gpu_all_in
grid_mw = it_load_mw * pue
print(f'~{gpus:,.0f} GPUs, needing ~{grid_mw:.0f} MW from the grid')

docs.title: 8.4 Colocation & Wholesale Leaders
docs.text:
Colocation companies build data centres and rent space, power and connectivity to many customers. Some focus on small 'retail' customers and rich interconnection; others build whole buildings for single big tenants (wholesale). Most of the largest are listed REITs or owned by private-equity and infrastructure investors.

Retail vs wholesale colocation

Retail colocation Wholesale / hyperscale Typical deal Racks, cages, suites Whole halls or buildings Size A few kW to a few MW Tens to hundreds of MW Contract Often 1-5 years Often 10-20 years Price per kW Higher Lower Key value Interconnection density Speed, scale, cost Examples Equinix, NTT, Global Switch QTS, Vantage, Aligned, AirTrunk

Same industry, very different contracts, buildings and customers.

Think of it like…

Retail colocation is like a serviced office block where many firms rent desks; wholesale is like a developer building a whole office tower for one big company.

Real-world example

Fictional fintech Ledgerly needs low-latency links to banks and clouds, so it rents four racks in a carrier-neutral retail facility with 300 networks on site. Meanwhile, fictional AI company Quanta Labs signs a 40 MW build-to-suit lease with a wholesale developer for a new campus. Both are colocation customers, but their contracts, prices and buildings look completely different.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Retail providers sell racks and cages with many interconnection options in city-centre hubs.
  2. Wholesale developers build large halls or campuses for one or a few hyperscale tenants.
  3. Ownership is often REITs (listed) or private-equity and infrastructure funds (private).
  4. Platforms change hands frequently, so always check the latest owner before quoting it.

Who uses it

Colocation providers employ many critical facilities engineers, technicians, sales engineers and customer-success staff, making them a common first employer.

Key takeaway

Equinix and Digital Realty are the two big listed data-centre REITs; most other big operators are privately owned by investment funds.

Going deeper

  • Ownership churns quickly: since 2021 private-equity and infrastructure investors have bought CyrusOne, QTS, Switch, AirTrunk and Aligned, so always check the latest owner and deal status.
  • Listed REITs such as Equinix, Digital Realty and Iron Mountain publish detailed quarterly reports on bookings, pricing, churn and capacity under construction, which make free training material.
  • Retail operators win on ecosystems: networks, clouds and internet exchanges inside one building make each new customer more valuable to the others.
  • Wholesale developers compete on power availability, delivery speed, land banks and the ability to finance gigawatt-scale campuses pre-leased to a few tenants.
  • Regional specialists such as Princeton Digital Group, Scala, Data4 and AirTrunk are major local employers; global brand names are only part of the jobs map.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Quoting company ownership from old articles; mergers and sales change owners frequently.
  • Assuming 'colocation' always means small racks; wholesale colocation leases entire buildings.
  • Comparing operators by number of sites alone; megawatts and interconnection reach matter more.

docs.title: 8.5 AI Cloud Builders (Neoclouds) & Giant AI Campuses
docs.text:
Since 2023, demand for AI has created a new kind of company, the 'neocloud', that rents out huge numbers of GPUs. At the same time, AI labs and cloud giants announced campuses measured in gigawatts, far bigger than traditional data centres. Many of these projects are partnerships between chip makers, cloud providers, investors and energy companies.

How a neocloud deal is built. The customer contract comes first; everything else is financed against it.

Think of it like…

Neoclouds are like equipment-hire firms that bought thousands of rare power tools early and rent them by the hour or year to builders who cannot get their own.

Real-world example

Fictional AI lab Corvid signs a three-year contract with fictional neocloud Kestrel Compute for 16,000 GPUs. Kestrel does not own a building, so it leases a 40 MW liquid-cooled hall from a developer and borrows against Corvid's contract to buy the servers. If Corvid's demand falls, Kestrel still owes rent and loan payments, which is why investors watch neocloud contracts closely.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An AI customer commits to a multi-year capacity contract.
  2. The neocloud uses that contract to raise debt and buy GPUs, networking and storage.
  3. It leases or builds liquid-cooled, high-density halls with fast power delivery.
  4. Clusters are installed, burned in and handed over; the customer pays per GPU-hour or per month.
  5. Gigawatt campuses repeat this at enormous scale, often with on-site or dedicated power.

Who uses it

AI infrastructure engineers, HPC technicians, electrical and mechanical engineers, and finance teams are heavily recruited by neoclouds and AI campus builders.

Key takeaway

Announced gigawatts are not the same as operating gigawatts: always ask whether a project is announced, under construction or energised.

Going deeper

  • Neocloud economics depend on utilisation and contract length: GPUs lose value quickly as new generations arrive, so lenders prefer long take-or-pay contracts with creditworthy customers.
  • Customer concentration is a key risk: a few AI labs or hyperscalers often provide most revenue, so one contract change can reshape a company's outlook.
  • Many neoclouds lease from developers or convert former crypto-mining sites, because those sites already have grid connections and electrical infrastructure.
  • Gigawatt AI campuses combine many buildings, on-site substations and sometimes on-site generation; they are delivered in phases, so energised capacity lags announced capacity by years.
  • Partnership structures are complex: chip makers invest in customers, customers invest in suppliers and clouds rent from neoclouds, so read filings to see who carries the financial risk.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating announced gigawatts as operating capacity; check the phase, energisation date and power source.
  • Assuming neoclouds own their buildings; many lease halls from developers or former crypto miners.
  • Quoting fast-moving deal values without dates; AI contracts are frequently revised, expanded or cancelled.

docs.title: Try it: Simple GPU-rental economics (illustrative numbers only)
docs.text:
# Python: monthly revenue and power for a rented GPU cluster
gpus = 16_000
price_per_gpu_hour = 2.20     # assumed contract price, USD
hours = 730                   # hours in an average month
kw_per_gpu_all_in = 1.8       # assumed IT power per GPU incl. network

revenue = gpus * price_per_gpu_hour * hours
it_mw = gpus * kw_per_gpu_all_in / 1000
print(f'Revenue ~ ${revenue/1e6:.1f}m per month for ~{it_mw:.0f} MW of IT load')

docs.title: 8.6 The World's Major Data Centre Markets
docs.text:
Data centres cluster in certain places, called markets, where power, fibre networks, land and customers come together. A few hubs such as Northern Virginia, Frankfurt and Singapore are famous, while new AI campuses are moving to wherever large amounts of power are available. Knowing the markets helps you understand where the jobs are.

Where data-centre capacity clusters. Growth is spreading from famous interconnection hubs to wherever power can be found.

Think of it like…

Markets are like airport hubs: once many airlines (networks) meet in one place, everyone else wants to be there too, until the runways (power) run out.

Real-world example

Fictional operator Northlight wants to build 100 MW. Its first choice, a famous city hub, has a five-year wait for grid power and strict planning rules. It instead picks a secondary market 300 km away where a utility can deliver power in two years and fibre routes already pass by. Latency-sensitive customers stay in the hub, while AI training moves to the new site.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Primary markets grew where internet exchanges and carriers met.
  2. Cloud regions followed, making those hubs even bigger.
  3. Power and land shortages pushed growth to secondary markets and new regions.
  4. AI training, which needs less low latency, moves to wherever gigawatts can be found.
  5. Governments now shape markets with grid rules, tax incentives, moratoriums and data-sovereignty laws.

Who uses it

Site selection teams, developers, brokers and job seekers all track markets; technician jobs are concentrated in these hubs.

Key takeaway

Memorise FLAP-D (Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, Dublin) for Europe and Northern Virginia as the world's largest market.

Going deeper

  • Markets are compared by operational MW, MW under construction, pre-leasing, vacancy, rents and absorption; brokers such as CBRE, JLL and Cushman & Wakefield publish these figures regularly.
  • Interconnection-rich hubs grew around internet exchanges: DE-CIX in Frankfurt, LINX in London, AMS-IX in Amsterdam and the carrier-dense campuses of Ashburn in Northern Virginia.
  • AI training is less latency-sensitive than user-facing services, so it moves to power-rich areas such as West Texas, the Nordics and the Middle East, while inference stays nearer users.
  • Data-sovereignty and localisation rules in India, the EU, the Gulf states and elsewhere push capacity into each country, creating local markets regardless of power prices.
  • Constraints shift growth quickly: grid limits, moratoria, tax-incentive changes and water rules can move demand to neighbouring regions within a few years, as Singapore's limits did for Johor.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming all growth stays in famous hubs; power scarcity is pushing builds to secondary and rural markets.
  • Ignoring latency: AI training can go remote, but trading, gaming and interconnection still need city hubs.
  • Quoting old market rankings; capacity league tables shift every year.

docs.title: 8.7 Power Equipment Vendors
docs.text:
A handful of global companies make most of the electrical equipment inside data centres: UPS systems, switchgear, transformers, power distribution and backup generators. Because AI campuses need so much of this kit, these vendors' factories, lead times and new products shape how fast the industry can grow. You will see their logos on almost every panel you work on.

Who supplies each link of the power chain. Most sites mix several brands along the chain, each with its own service team.

Think of it like…

These vendors are like the few big car makers: every road (data centre) is full of their products, and when their factories are busy, everyone waits.

Real-world example

Fictional developer Brightfield orders equipment for a 60 MW building. It buys medium-voltage switchgear and transformers from one supplier, UPS from another, and twenty 3 MW diesel generators from a third. The transformers have the longest wait, so they are ordered 24 months before handover. Technicians later attend each vendor's training so they can operate and maintain the kit safely.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Designers specify equipment by rating, redundancy and standards compliance.
  2. Procurement compares vendors on price, lead time, efficiency and local service support.
  3. Factory acceptance tests (FAT) are witnessed before shipping.
  4. Vendor field engineers support installation, commissioning and maintenance contracts.
  5. Site teams receive vendor training and spare-parts kits.

Who uses it

Electrical engineers, critical facilities technicians, commissioning agents and procurement teams deal with these vendors daily; many also hire field service engineers.

Key takeaway

Learn at least one UPS family and one generator make in depth; interviewers love it when you can describe a real unit's modes and alarms.

Going deeper

  • Long-lead items are the bottleneck: large power transformers, MV switchgear, generators and gas turbines have faced waits of many months to years, so developers reserve factory slots early.
  • Vendors increasingly sell integrated prefabricated power modules, e-houses and skids, shifting work from the construction site to factories and witnessed factory acceptance tests.
  • Service networks matter as much as hardware: response times, local spare stock and trained field engineers often decide which UPS or generator brand wins a tender.
  • AI power trends are reshaping product lines: 800 V DC and ±400 V DC distribution, solid-state transformers, battery-backup shelves and grid-interactive UPS all appear on vendor roadmaps.
  • Interviewers value brand fluency: knowing a Liebert, Galaxy or Eaton 93-series UPS, or a Cummins or Caterpillar generator controller, signals hands-on readiness.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Confusing Siemens AG with Siemens Energy, or GE Vernova with GE Aerospace; they are separate listed companies.
  • Ordering long-lead equipment late; lead times can exceed the whole construction period.
  • Assuming all UPS units behave the same; operating modes, bypass logic and alarms differ by vendor and model.

docs.title: Try it: Generator count for a building (worked N+1 example)
docs.text:
# Python: how many 3 MW gensets for 24 MW of facility load at N+1?
import math
load_mw = 24.0
gen_mw = 3.0          # rated output per genset (example)
derate = 0.9          # allow for altitude/temperature (assumed)
n = math.ceil(load_mw / (gen_mw * derate))
print(f'N = {n}, N+1 = {n+1} generators')

docs.title: 8.8 Cooling, Rack & Cabling Vendors
docs.text:
Another set of companies makes the cooling plant, racks and cables. HVAC giants supply chillers and air handlers, specialists build liquid-cooling systems for AI racks, and structured-cabling firms supply the copper and fibre that connect everything. The liquid-cooling market has seen many acquisitions as big firms race to offer AI-ready solutions.

Who supplies an AI hall's cooling and connectivity. Plant, liquid loops, racks and fibre usually come from different vendors that must be integrated.

Think of it like…

If the data centre were a human body, the cooling vendors make the heart and lungs, and the cabling vendors make the nerves.

Real-world example

Fictional neocloud Kestrel Compute fits out a 20 MW AI hall. It buys air-cooled chillers from an HVAC major, in-row CDUs from a liquid-cooling specialist and 4,000 km of fibre plus pre-terminated trunks from a cabling vendor. The cabling vendor's design team plans every cable route so the GPU cluster can be wired in weeks instead of months.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Mechanical engineers size chillers, air handlers and liquid loops for the IT load.
  2. Liquid-cooling vendors provide CDUs, cold plates or immersion tanks matched to the servers.
  3. Rack and containment vendors supply cabinets, aisle containment and rack cooling.
  4. Cabling vendors provide copper, fibre, connectors and pathways, often pre-terminated.
  5. All are tested together during commissioning before the IT goes live.

Who uses it

Mechanical engineers, cooling technicians, structured-cabling installers and data-centre technicians use these products every day.

Key takeaway

Expect interview questions on why AI racks need liquid cooling; name a CDU and a cold-plate vendor and explain what each does.

Going deeper

  • HVAC majors supply the plant (chillers, cooling towers, air handlers) while liquid-cooling specialists supply CDUs, manifolds and cold plates; AI halls need both working together.
  • Consolidation is rapid: Schneider took a majority stake in Motivair, Vertiv bought CoolTera, Flex bought JetCool, Ecolab bought CoolIT and Eaton agreed to buy Boyd's thermal business.
  • Server makers and GPU vendors publish reference designs listing qualified CDUs, cold plates and coolants, so warranty and compatibility strongly shape vendor choice.
  • AI clusters need many times more fibre than traditional halls because every GPU connects to high-speed back-end networks, driving demand for high-fibre-count cables and pre-terminated trunks.
  • Immersion cooling has its own specialist suppliers, but direct-to-chip cold plates have become the mainstream choice for current GPU rack designs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming one vendor supplies the whole cooling chain; chillers, CDUs and cold plates often come from different firms.
  • Ignoring coolant and wetted-material compatibility when mixing CDU and cold-plate vendors.
  • Quoting pre-acquisition company names in interviews; check current ownership first.

docs.title: 8.9 Careers I: Facilities, Engineering & Construction Roles
docs.text:
Behind every data centre is a team that keeps the power and cooling running 24 hours a day, plus the people who design and build new sites. These 'critical facilities' jobs suit people with electrical, mechanical or building skills, and many start as technicians. There is a well-known shortage of skilled staff, so good candidates are in demand.

A facilities career ladder. Most people climb by proving safe, procedure-driven work at each level, not by certificates alone.

Think of it like…

The facilities team is like the engineering crew on a ship: passengers (the IT) never see them, but without them the ship stops.

Real-world example

Fictional ex-electrician Priya joins a colocation site as a critical facilities technician on a four-on, four-off shift pattern. Her day starts with a handover, then a walk-round reading UPS, generator and chiller panels, followed by a planned task: assisting a vendor with a UPS battery test under an approved MOP. After two years and a certification she becomes a critical facilities engineer leading changes herself.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start as a technician or apprentice, learning rounds, alarms and safe working.
  2. Specialise in electrical, mechanical or controls systems.
  3. Lead maintenance and changes as an engineer, writing and executing MOPs.
  4. Move into shift lead, site operations manager, design, commissioning or construction roles.
  5. Senior paths include regional operations director or engineering design lead.

Who uses it

Electricians, HVAC technicians, military veterans, building-services and engineering graduates commonly move into these roles.

Key takeaway

Safety and procedure discipline matter more than knowing everything; say in interviews that you would stop and escalate rather than guess.

Going deeper

  • Typical shift patterns include 4-on-4-off and other rotating 12-hour schedules covering nights, weekends and holidays; shift allowances and overtime are common in facilities roles.
  • Qualification routes differ by country: US technicians usually need NFPA 70E training and may hold state electrical licences, while UK roles favour 18th Edition and authorised-person HV training.
  • Progression usually depends on demonstrated MOP execution, incident handling and system knowledge; many employers run internal qualification levels for each electrical and mechanical system.
  • Construction and commissioning roles boomed with AI campuses and often pay well but involve travel and project-to-project work, whereas operations roles offer more stability.
  • The industry reports persistent staff shortages, so career-changers from the trades, the military and building services are actively recruited and trained.
  • Useful early skills: reading single-line diagrams, understanding UPS and ATS operation, chilled-water basics, BMS alarm handling and writing clear shift handovers.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Overstating experience with high-voltage switching; employers check authorisation and will test your knowledge.
  • Ignoring shift-work realities; nights, weekends and holidays are normal in operations roles.
  • Chasing certificates before hands-on experience; employers value safe practical work first.

docs.title: 8.10 Careers II: IT, Operations & Business Roles
docs.text:
Not every data-centre job involves generators and chillers. Many people work with the servers, network cables and software inside, while others plan capacity, sell space, manage energy or choose new sites. AI clusters have added new roles for people who can build and run huge GPU systems.

IT and business career paths. The technician role is a hub: most IT-side careers can start there.

Think of it like…

If facilities staff keep the stadium's lights and turf in shape, these roles are the players, coaches, ticket office and stadium planners.

Real-world example

Fictional graduate Tomás starts as a data centre technician at a cloud provider, swapping failed drives, replacing memory and running fibre patches from work tickets. He learns Linux and networking in the evenings and earns a networking certification. Two years later he moves into a deployment engineer role, bringing new GPU racks online, and later becomes an AI cluster engineer.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start in a hands-on technician, NOC or cabling role.
  2. Learn Linux, networking and a scripting language such as Python.
  3. Specialise: networking, deployment, capacity, DCIM, AI/HPC or sustainability.
  4. Business-minded people move into sales engineering, account management or site selection.
  5. Senior roles include data centre architect, infrastructure manager or head of capacity.

Who uses it

IT support staff, computer-science and networking students, career changers and business graduates all find routes in here.

Key takeaway

Data centre technician jobs at cloud providers are a common first step for beginners; list hands-on lab work and any safety training on your CV.

Going deeper

  • Hyperscale technician roles often involve high-volume break-fix work driven by tickets and automated diagnostics, while colocation roles involve more customer contact and remote-hands requests.
  • Linux, basic networking (VLANs, BGP, optics), scripting in Python or Bash and server-management interfaces such as BMC, IPMI and Redfish are the skills that unlock promotion.
  • AI cluster roles add GPU health checks, InfiniBand or RoCE fabric troubleshooting, cabling at massive scale and job schedulers such as Slurm or Kubernetes.
  • Business roles still need technical literacy: sales engineers, capacity planners and site-selection managers must read single-line diagrams, density figures and lease terms.
  • Sustainability and energy roles now need regulatory knowledge, such as EU reporting, CSRD and the GHG Protocol, alongside metering and data-analysis skills.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Ignoring the physical side; technician roles involve lifting, standing for long periods and shift work.
  • Neglecting documentation; accurate tickets and asset records are judged as closely as technical fixes.
  • Assuming business roles need no technical knowledge; credibility with customers depends on it.

docs.title: 8.11 Certifications & Training That Employers Recognise
docs.text:
Certifications are courses with exams that prove you know a subject to a recognised level. In data centres, some cover the whole facility, some cover design standards or cabling, and some cover the IT inside. Safety and electrical qualifications are often legally required before you may touch certain equipment.

A certification roadmap. Build from the bottom up, and keep safety training current at every stage.

Think of it like…

Certifications are like a driving licence plus extra endorsements: the basic licence gets you on the road, and endorsements let you drive bigger vehicles.

Real-world example

Fictional student Amara plans her first year: CompTIA A+ in three months, then an entry data centre course such as CDCP or CDCTP while applying for technician jobs. After landing a job, her employer pays for NFPA 70E safety training and later an operations course. She keeps a spreadsheet of exam dates, costs and renewal deadlines.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start with fundamentals: A+, Network+ or an entry data-centre course.
  2. Add mandatory safety training for your country and role.
  3. Choose a specialist path: operations, design, cabling, electrical or AI infrastructure.
  4. Let employers fund expensive courses once you are hired.
  5. Track renewals; many certifications expire after a few years.

Who uses it

Job seekers, technicians aiming for promotion, engineers moving into design, and managers proving competence to customers and auditors.

Key takeaway

A cheap fundamentals certificate plus hands-on experience beats an expensive design credential you cannot yet use; always check the current exam code before booking.

Going deeper

  • Entry certificates such as CompTIA A+, Network+, CDCP and CDCTP show vocabulary and commitment; they rarely replace experience but help CVs pass automated screening.
  • Uptime Institute's ATD, ATS and AOS are aimed at professionals working with Tier certification, so most people take them once employed, often with employer funding.
  • BICSI credentials (Installer, Technician, RCDD, DCDC) are respected in cabling and design; RCDD requires qualifying industry experience before you can sit the exam.
  • Safety training is often a legal or contractual prerequisite: NFPA 70E and OSHA Outreach cards in the US, and electrical qualifications such as the 18th Edition in the UK.
  • Vendor and AI certifications from NVIDIA, cloud providers and network vendors signal skills for GPU and network roles; exam codes and validity periods change often.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Paying for expensive design certifications before you can use them; start with fundamentals and safety.
  • Letting certifications lapse; many require periodic renewal, fees or continuing-education credits to stay valid.
  • Booking outdated exam versions; check current exam codes on the provider's website first.

docs.title: 8.12 Learning Resources, News & Communities
docs.text:
The data-centre industry changes every month, so professionals keep learning through news sites, research reports, free vendor courses and industry groups. Many of the best resources are free. Joining communities and attending local events is also the fastest way to meet people who hire.

A weekly learning routine. Small, regular habits beat occasional cramming, and the networking step is what leads to referrals.

Think of it like…

Building your learning routine is like going to the gym: a little reading every week beats cramming once a year.

Real-world example

Fictional career-changer Jordan sets a weekly routine: 20 minutes of trade news every morning, one vendor white paper each weekend and one recorded conference talk on Wednesdays. He posts questions on an online forum and attends a local chapter meeting of an industry association. Three months later a member he met there refers him for a technician vacancy.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Follow two or three trade-news sources for daily headlines.
  2. Read annual surveys to understand big trends and statistics.
  3. Work through free vendor courses and white papers on power and cooling.
  4. Watch conference talks to see how leading operators design sites.
  5. Join a community or association and attend events to build contacts.

Who uses it

Students, job seekers and experienced engineers alike; hiring managers often ask what you read to stay current.

Key takeaway

Mention one recent industry story and one survey statistic in an interview to show genuine interest.

Going deeper

  • Uptime Institute's annual surveys provide citable statistics on outages, PUE, staffing and rack density; read the free summaries and note one figure to use in interviews.
  • Schneider Electric's white papers and free online courses explain UPS topologies, containment, economisers and total cost of ownership in an accessible style, making them ideal first reading.
  • Trade news from DCD, Data Center Frontier and Data Center Knowledge shows who is building where, which helps you target applications at companies that are hiring.
  • Associations such as 7x24 Exchange and AFCOM run local chapters and student or young-professional events, often the fastest way to meet hiring managers.
  • Listed operators' filings and investor presentations are free, detailed and reliable sources on capacity, pricing and strategy.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Relying on social-media rumours; verify claims with primary sources such as filings and official announcements.
  • Only reading and never building notes or labs; employers want evidence you applied what you learned.
  • Paying for courses before using the free vendor and association material.

docs.title: 8.13 Interview Questions & How to Break In
docs.text:
Most data-centre interviews mix technical questions about power, cooling and safety with questions about how you behave under pressure. You do not need years of experience to start, but you must show safe habits, curiosity and the basics. Many people enter from the military, the electrical or HVAC trades, or IT helpdesk jobs.

From zero to first offer. Evidence of safe habits and genuine curiosity matters more than years of experience.

Think of it like…

An interview is like a driving test: they want to see you know the rules of the road and stay calm, not that you can race.

Real-world example

Fictional candidate Leila is asked: 'The utility fails at 3 a.m. — what happens?' She explains: UPS batteries carry the IT load instantly, generators start and stabilise within seconds, the ATS transfers load to them, and the team follows the emergency procedure and logs everything. She adds she would never bypass a step without the shift lead. The interviewer later says that last sentence won her the job.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Revise the core concepts: power chain, redundancy, PUE, airflow and safety.
  2. Prepare three STAR stories about problem-solving, teamwork and following procedure.
  3. Build a small home lab and keep a learning log or portfolio.
  4. Apply widely to technician, NOC and cabling roles; tailor your CV to each.
  5. After the interview, follow up and keep studying whatever you could not answer.

Who uses it

Anyone applying for technician, engineer or operations roles, and interviewers preparing questions.

Key takeaway

When unsure, say what you would check and who you would escalate to; data-centre employers value safe caution over confident guessing.

Going deeper

  • Technical interviews often include a whiteboard power-chain drawing, a utility-failure scenario, redundancy definitions and a PUE calculation; practise each aloud in under two minutes.
  • Behavioural questions test safety culture: describe a time you stopped work, escalated a concern or followed a procedure under pressure, using the STAR structure.
  • A portfolio with a simple 2N single-line diagram, a home-lab write-up and notes from a vendor course gives interviewers concrete evidence beyond the CV.
  • Veteran, trade and helpdesk routes are recognised entry paths; translate past experience into data-centre language, such as 'maintained generators' or 'worked to written procedures'.
  • Large employers run structured hiring with online assessments and panel interviews; read the job description's required skills and reflect its wording honestly in your CV.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Guessing when unsure; say what you would check and who you would escalate to.
  • Leaving safety out of answers; mention LOTO, PPE and MOPs whenever you describe hands-on work.
  • Sending one generic CV everywhere; tailor it to technician, NOC or cabling roles.

docs.text: Name What it does Example Q: Explain N, N+1 and 2NClassic technical question · Concept · Current · General N is just enough capacity; N+1 adds one spare unit; 2N duplicates the whole system on two independent paths. Answer with an example: four chillers needed, five installed is N+1; two full UPS systems is 2N. Q: What is PUE?The Green Grid; ISO/IEC 30134-2 · Metric · Current · Sustainability Total facility energy divided by IT energy; lower is better and 1.0 is the theoretical ideal. 1,300 kW facility for 1,000 kW of IT gives PUE 1.3; mention it is measured over a year. Q: Walk me through the power chainClassic technical question · Practice · Current · Electrical Trace power from grid to chip: utility, substation, transformer, switchgear, UPS, PDU, RPP, rack PDU, server PSU. Draw it on a whiteboard and add where generators and the ATS connect. Q: What happens when the utility fails?Classic scenario question · Procedure · Current · Electrical UPS carries load instantly, generators start, ATS transfers, cooling restarts, staff follow the EOP and log events. Mention you would check generators are carrying load, fuel levels and UPS battery recharge afterwards. Q: Hot vs cold aisle containmentClassic technical question · Concept · Current · Mechanical Containment physically separates cold supply air from hot exhaust so they do not mix, improving efficiency. Explain that cold-aisle containment encloses the inlet aisle while hot-aisle containment captures the exhaust. Q: What are a MOP, SOP and EOP?Operations procedures · Document · Current · Operations Method of Procedure for a specific change; Standard Operating Procedure for routine tasks; Emergency Operating Procedure for failures. Say you follow a MOP line by line, with a second person checking, and stop if anything differs. Q: LOTO and arc flashOSHA 1910.147; NFPA 70E · Procedure · Current · Electrical Lockout/tagout isolates and locks energy sources; arc flash is a violent electrical explosion that PPE and de-energising prevent. Explain you would verify zero energy with a tested meter before touching any conductor. STAR behavioural answersInterview technique · Practice · Current · General Answer behavioural questions with Situation, Task, Action and Result, keeping each story under two minutes. 'Tell me about a mistake': describe a missed step, how you reported it and the checklist you then created. Home labSelf-study · Practice · Current · IT A small set-up at home, such as an old server or Raspberry Pi, to practise Linux, monitoring and cabling. Install Linux on a used server, read its sensors with ipmitool and graph temperatures. Learning portfolioSelf-study · Resource · Current · General A simple online log or document showing labs, certifications, diagrams and notes you have produced. Share a one-page drawing of a 2N power design and a write-up of your home lab. Military veteran routeEmployer veteran programmes · Practice · Current · General Veterans with electrical, mechanical or IT experience are highly valued for discipline and procedure-following. A former navy electrician moves into a critical facilities engineer role within months. Trades routeElectricians, HVAC and building-services technicians · Practice · Current · Facilities Qualified tradespeople can move straight into facilities roles after learning data-centre specifics. An HVAC technician joins a site's mechanical team and learns chillers and CRAHs. IT helpdesk routeIT support and NOC roles · Practice · Current · IT Helpdesk experience with hardware, tickets and customers maps well to data centre technician work. A helpdesk analyst with A+ applies for a cloud provider's technician role. Apprenticeships & college programmesEmployers, colleges and government schemes · Resource · Current · General Paid apprenticeships and college partnerships train beginners while they work toward qualifications. A school leaver joins a two-year data-centre engineering apprenticeship with a colocation operator. Q: Tier III vs Tier IV?Classic technical question · Concept · Current · General Tier III is concurrently maintainable: any component can be maintained without shutdown. Tier IV also survives any single unplanned failure. Add that Tier IV usually needs active 2N paths with compartmentalisation, and that neither Tier guarantees zero downtime. Q: Why do AI racks need liquid cooling?Modern technical question · Concept · Emerging · Mechanical Racks of 100 kW or more produce more heat than air can practically remove; liquid carries far more heat per volume directly from chips. Mention cold plates, CDUs and facility water loops, and that a GB200 NVL72 rack draws roughly 120-140 kW.

docs.title: 8.14 Industry Trends to Watch (2026 and Beyond)
docs.text:
AI has turned data centres from quiet back-office buildings into one of the world's biggest construction and energy stories. Racks are getting far more power-hungry, liquid cooling is becoming normal and finding electricity is now the hardest part of any project. Some ideas, like data centres in space, are still experiments.

How AI changed rack power. In under a decade, typical new AI racks went from single-digit kW to well over 100 kW.

Think of it like…

The industry is like a city that suddenly needs ten times more water: plumbing, reservoirs and rules all have to change at once.

Real-world example

Fictional operator Ironbridge planned its 2022 halls for 10 kW racks with air cooling. By 2026 a customer asks for 130 kW AI racks, so Ironbridge retrofits one hall with CDUs and liquid loops and designs its next building for 200 kW+ racks. Because the grid connection is years away, it adds on-site gas generation and a battery system, and signs a long-term clean-power contract.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Track rack densities in new GPU systems and their power and cooling needs.
  2. Watch how utilities, regulators and governments respond to huge new loads.
  3. Follow energy deals: gas, nuclear, renewables, storage and fuel cells.
  4. Note which technologies move from 'emerging' to standard practice.
  5. Separate firm, funded projects from announcements and speculation.

Who uses it

Everyone in the industry, especially designers, investors, energy managers and job seekers choosing which skills to learn.

Key takeaway

Liquid cooling, high-voltage power distribution and grid/energy skills are the safest bets for a future-proof career.

Going deeper

  • Density drives everything: higher kW per rack changes floor loading, distribution voltages, cooling technology and the skills operators need on every shift.
  • Energy has become strategic: developers sign gas, nuclear, geothermal and storage deals and some build on-site plants, so energy-market knowledge is a career differentiator.
  • Regulation and community scrutiny are rising together, with large-load tariffs, water and noise rules and reporting duties shaping where and how campuses are built.
  • Supply chains for GPUs, high-bandwidth memory, transformers and turbines can delay projects more than construction itself, making procurement and planning key roles.
  • Speculative ideas such as orbital data centres attract headlines; separate funded, under-construction projects from announcements when judging which trends will create jobs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating every announcement as certain; many projects are delayed, resized or cancelled.
  • Assuming air-cooling skills are obsolete; most general-purpose IT will remain air-cooled for years.
  • Ignoring energy and policy trends; they increasingly decide where data centres, and jobs, appear.

docs.title: Try it: How much coolant does a 130 kW AI rack need? (worked example)
docs.text:
# Python: coolant flow = heat / (specific heat x temperature rise)
heat_w = 130_000          # rack heat load, W
cp = 4186                 # J/(kg.K), water (glycol mixes are lower)
delta_t = 10              # K temperature rise across the rack
kg_per_s = heat_w / (cp * delta_t)
print(f'{kg_per_s:.2f} kg/s = about {kg_per_s*60:.0f} litres per minute')

docs.title: Chapter 5: IT, Networking & AI Clusters Inside the Data Centre
docs.text: Power, cooling and buildings exist for one reason: to keep the IT equipment running. This chapter opens the racks to show the servers, GPUs, storage, networks and cables inside, how giant AI clusters are wired together, how virtualisation and edge sites fit in, and what happens to hardware at the end of its life. It gives facilities and IT students a shared language for the white space.

docs.title: 5.1 Servers: The Computers That Fill the Racks
docs.text:
A server is a computer built to run all day, every day, doing work for many other computers or people at once. Data-centre servers are flat metal boxes that slide into racks, with no screen or keyboard, and they are managed remotely over the network. Inside you find the same basic parts as a PC (processor, memory, storage, network card), just more of them, built for reliability.

Inside a two-socket 2U server. Everything except the motherboard is duplicated or hot-swappable, and the BMC lets you manage it all remotely.

Think of it like…

If your laptop is a family car, a server is a delivery van: less pretty, built to carry heavy loads around the clock, and serviced by a fleet manager rather than its driver.

Real-world example

Kestrel Insurance replaces 40 five-year-old 2U servers with 12 new 2U servers that each have two 96-core processors and 1.5 TB of memory. Because each new box does the work of about three old ones, the rack count drops from four to two and power falls from roughly 24 kW to 14 kW. Engineers never visit the racks for setup: they mount the servers, cable them, and finish everything through each server's remote management port.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose a form factor: 1U/2U rack servers for general work, blades or multi-node chassis for density, 4U-10U boxes for GPUs.
  2. Pick the processor family (x86 from Intel or AMD, or Arm) and the number of sockets, cores and memory channels.
  3. Add memory (DDR5 RDIMMs), local drives (usually NVMe SSDs) and network cards (25-400 Gb/s).
  4. Fit redundant hot-swap power supplies and fans so one failure does not stop the server.
  5. Connect the BMC port to a separate management network so the server can be powered, monitored and reinstalled remotely.
  6. Install firmware updates, an operating system or hypervisor, then hand the server to the application team.

Who uses it

Data-centre technicians rack and cable servers, while system administrators, cloud engineers and hardware engineers at hyperscalers, colos, banks and universities configure and support them.

Key takeaway

Memorise the anatomy: CPU sockets, DIMM slots, drive bays, PCIe slots, OCP NIC slot, dual PSUs and the BMC port — interviewers love asking you to name the parts of a server.

Going deeper

  • Space is rarely the real limit: a 42U rack has room for 40 1U servers, but power and cooling budgets of 10-20 kW usually cap it at 10-20 modern servers.
  • Single-socket servers built on high-core-count EPYC chips are increasingly popular: they avoid slower cross-socket (NUMA) memory access and can reduce software licences charged per socket.
  • Memory bandwidth depends on populating every channel: EPYC 9005 and Xeon 6900P platforms have 12 DDR5 channels per socket, and empty or mismatched channels can cut bandwidth substantially.
  • Drive form factors are moving from 2.5-inch U.2 to EDSFF (E1.S, E3.S), which fit more NVMe drives per U and cool better; a PCIe 5.0 x4 SSD reads at roughly 14 GB/s.
  • Power supplies run as 1+1 redundant pairs on A and B feeds; 80 PLUS Titanium units reach about 96% efficiency at half load, and every watt saved also saves cooling.
  • Security starts below the operating system: a hardware root of trust checks firmware at boot, and confidential-computing features (AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX) encrypt VM memory even from the host administrator.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Planning servers by rack units alone; a rack of 1U servers can blow its power budget, so plan kW per rack first, then space.
  • Mixing DIMM sizes or leaving memory channels empty to save money; it lowers bandwidth, so install identical modules in every channel.
  • Plugging both power supplies into the same PDU; that removes redundancy, so always split them across the A and B feeds.
  • Leaving BMCs on the production network with default passwords; isolate them on the out-of-band network and use unique credentials.
