docs.title: 6.7 MOPs, SOPs, EOPs & Written Procedures
docs.text:
Data centres run on written procedures so that every risky task is done the same safe way, whoever is on shift. A MOP (Method of Procedure) is a step-by-step plan for one specific job, an SOP (Standard Operating Procedure) covers routine tasks, and an EOP (Emergency Operating Procedure) tells staff exactly what to do when something fails. Procedures are reviewed, approved and followed line by line.

MOP vs SOP vs EOP

MOP SOP EOP Purpose One-off risky task Routine repeated task Respond to a failure Example Replace an A-side breaker Daily rounds, filter change Utility power loss Written Before each job Once, reviewed yearly In advance, then drilled Approval Peer review, chief engineer, CAB Site management Site management Style Long, numbered, hold points Short checklist Short decision steps

The same site needs all three, written in different styles for different moments.

Think of it like…

A MOP is like a pilot's checklist: even experienced pilots read and tick each line, because skipping one step can be catastrophic.

Real-world example

Engineer Aisha at the fictional Northgate DC must replace a breaker on the A-side switchboard. Her 34-step MOP lists pre-checks (B-side healthy, generator fuel above 75%, customers notified), each switching step with expected readings, hold points where a second engineer verifies, and a back-out plan if the B-side alarms. Two reviewers sign it, the change board approves it, and on the night she initials each step as she goes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the task and its risk; choose the right document type (MOP, SOP, EOP or ARP).
  2. Write clear numbered steps with expected results, hold points, safety notes and a back-out plan.
  3. Peer review by another engineer, then approval by the chief engineer (and customers or change board if needed).
  4. Brief the team, perform the steps with a second person verifying critical actions, and initial each step.
  5. Record deviations, close out, and update the procedure with lessons learned.

Who uses it

Every critical facilities engineer writes and follows procedures; technical writers and operations managers maintain the procedure library.

Key takeaway

Never improvise during a MOP: if reality does not match the expected result, stop at a hold point and use the back-out plan.

Going deeper

  • A good MOP covers scope, risk level, affected systems and customers, staff and tools, pre-checks, numbered steps with expected readings, hold points, back-out steps, post-checks and sign-off fields.
  • Write one action per step using the exact equipment labels on site, for example 'Open breaker UPS-A-OUT-02', so the document matches the labels and the single-line diagram.
  • Uptime Institute surveys find most human-error outages involve staff not following procedures or procedures that were wrong, so writing and enforcing procedures is a core reliability skill.
  • EOPs are short, decision-tree style and often posted at the equipment; they are drilled so staff can act within minutes, for example starting a generator manually if auto-start fails.
  • Walk the MOP down on site before approval to confirm that labels, breaker positions, access and tools match the paperwork.
  • Under document control every procedure carries a version, owner and review date, often annual; superseded copies are withdrawn and printed copies are checked against the master before use.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Re-using an old MOP without walking down the site; equipment and labels change, so verify every step in the field.
  • Skipping the back-out plan because 'it will go fine'; every MOP needs a tested way back.
  • Pressing on after an unexpected reading; stop at the hold point and escalate instead of improvising.

docs.title: Try it: Sample MOP skeleton (YAML)
docs.text:
mop:
  id: MOP-ELEC-042
  title: Replace breaker Q7 on switchboard SWB-A
  risk: High   # loss of redundancy during work
  author: A. Rahman
  reviewer: L. Chen
  approver: Chief Engineer
  pre_checks:
    - SWB-B healthy, no active alarms
    - Generators available, fuel > 75%
    - Customers notified 10 working days ahead
  steps:
    - {n: 1, action: Confirm load on Q7 = 0 A via EPMS, verify: 2nd engineer}
    - {n: 2, action: Open Q7 and apply LOTO, verify: 2nd engineer}
    - {n: 3, action: HOLD POINT - test for absence of voltage}
  back_out:
    - Stop work, restore Q7 per steps 2-1 in reverse, call chief engineer
  sign_off: [technician, verifier, shift_lead]

docs.title: Key equipment, standards, metrics, vendors & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example MOP (Method of Procedure)Industry practice · Document · Current · Operations A detailed, approved step-by-step plan for a specific non-routine task such as maintenance or a change on live systems. A 40-step MOP covers transferring a UPS to maintenance bypass for its annual service. SOP (Standard Operating Procedure)Industry practice · Document · Current · Operations Instructions for routine, repeated tasks performed the same way every time. The SOP for daily rounds lists every reading to record in each plant room. EOP (Emergency Operating Procedure)Industry practice · Document · Current · Operations Pre-written actions for failures, such as utility loss, chiller trip or fire alarm, to restore safe operation fast. The 'Generator fails to start' EOP tells the engineer which panel to check and how to start manually. ARP (Alarm Response Procedure)Industry practice · Document · Current · Operations Short instructions attached to a specific alarm telling the operator what it means and what to do first. The ARP for 'CRAH-12 high supply temp' says check fan status, then chilled-water valve, then call mechanical. Back-out (rollback) planMOP section · Procedure · Current · Operations Steps to safely return to the original state if the work goes wrong or results differ from those expected. If the new breaker will not close, the back-out plan restores the old one within 20 minutes. Hold pointMOP practice · Concept · Current · Operations A marked step where work stops until a check is confirmed or permission is given to continue. Work halts at step 12 until a second engineer confirms zero voltage with a tested meter. Two-person rule (verify & witness)Industry practice · Practice · Current · Operations A second qualified person checks critical actions before and as they happen, to catch mistakes. One engineer reads the step aloud and points at the breaker; the other confirms the label before it is operated. Peer review & approvalIndustry practice · Practice · Current · Operations Independent review of a procedure by another engineer, then formal sign-off by a responsible manager. A reviewer spots that a MOP opens the wrong bus-coupler and the step is corrected before approval. Pre-task briefing (toolbox talk)Industry practice · Practice · Current · Operations A short meeting before work to walk through steps, hazards, roles and stop conditions. Five minutes before switching, the team agrees who reads, who operates and who watches the EPMS. Switching programmeElectrical safety-rules practice (e.g. HV authorised persons) · Document · Current · Electrical A written, checked sequence of switching operations, isolation points and earths for a planned electrical outage, prepared before any switching starts. Before UPS-A maintenance, the authorised engineer writes a 12-step switching programme, which a second engineer checks against the single-line diagram. Sequence of operations (SOO)Controls design document · Document · Current · Mechanical Describes exactly how automatic controls should behave in every mode, such as a chiller plant switching to free cooling. Testing reveals the BMS does not follow the SOO for pump changeover, so the logic is fixed. docs.title: 6.8 Change Management
docs.text:
Change management is the process for deciding whether, when and how to change anything in the data centre, from a firmware update to replacing a transformer. Each change is described, assessed for risk, approved and scheduled before anyone starts. This matters because many outages happen during planned work.

From change request to review. Most of the risk is removed before the work starts, at the classification and CAB steps.

Think of it like…

It is like air traffic control for work: nobody takes off until their plan is checked, a slot is free and nothing else risky is using the same runway.

Real-world example

At the fictional Kestrel Colo, three changes are requested for the same Saturday: UPS-B firmware, a chiller valve replacement and a customer's rack power upgrade. The change advisory board scores them and sees that UPS-B and the chiller work both reduce redundancy at once. It moves the chiller job to the following week, approves the others, and customers on UPS-B get ten working days' notice through the portal.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Someone raises a change request describing what, why, when, the risk and the MOP.
  2. The change is classified (standard, normal or emergency) and risk-scored.
  3. A change advisory board reviews conflicts, timing and readiness, then approves, rejects or reschedules.
  4. Affected customers and teams are notified; the work is done in the agreed window.
  5. The change is closed with a review: did it succeed, and what was learned?

Who uses it

Change managers, operations managers, engineers and colocation customer-service teams take part; ITIL knowledge is often requested in job adverts.

Key takeaway

Interviewers like the phrase 'no change without a MOP, no MOP without review, no work without approval'.

Going deeper

  • Risk scoring usually multiplies impact (customers or redundancy affected) by likelihood (complexity, history); the score sets the approval level, from pre-approved standard changes to CAB plus senior sign-off.
  • Changes that reduce redundancy, such as running on one UPS side or with a chiller out, create 'at-risk' periods; good CABs never overlap them and confirm the remaining path is healthy first.
  • Colocation contracts often require several business days' notice, commonly 5-10, for planned work that could affect customers, with emergency work notified as soon as practicable.
  • ITIL 4 calls the practice 'change enablement' and lets low-risk standard changes flow without a CAB, freeing the board to focus on genuinely risky work.
  • The CrowdStrike outage of 19 July 2024 showed the danger of pushing one change to everything at once; staged rollouts and canaries are change-management controls.
  • Track change success rate and changes that caused incidents; trends reveal weak procedures, rushed approvals or teams that need training.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using emergency changes as a shortcut; they still need approval and a review afterwards.
  • Approving changes one at a time in isolation; check the forward schedule for overlapping redundancy reductions.
  • Closing a change without verifying success; post-checks and monitoring must confirm normal operation.

docs.title: Try it: Simple change risk score (Python)
docs.text:
impact = {'none':1,'single customer':2,'reduced redundancy':3,'whole hall':5}
likelihood = {'routine':1,'some complexity':2,'first time':3}
risk = impact['reduced redundancy'] * likelihood['first time']
level = 'High - CAB + director' if risk >= 9 else 'Medium - CAB' if risk >= 4 else 'Low - standard change'
print(risk, level)   # 9 High - CAB + director

docs.title: 6.9 Commissioning: Levels 1 to 5
docs.text:
Commissioning is the careful testing that proves a new (or upgraded) data centre works as designed before any real servers depend on it. It happens in five levels, from checking equipment at the factory to switching off the incoming power to the whole building on purpose and watching everything respond. Problems found now are far cheaper than problems found after customers move in.

Commissioning Levels 1 to 5. Each level must pass before the next starts, and Level 5 is the only one that tests everything together.

Think of it like…

It is like testing a new aeroplane: parts are checked at the factory, systems are checked on the ground, and finally test pilots fly it through emergencies before passengers board.

Real-world example

The fictional Fernhill campus builds a 24 MW hall. Engineers witness UPS and generator tests at the factories (Level 1), check installation on site (Level 2), start each unit (Level 3) and test each system alone (Level 4). In Level 5, 24 MW of load banks heat the hall while the team cuts utility power. One generator fails to synchronise, so the fault is fixed and the test repeated before handover.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Level 1: factory witness tests prove major equipment meets its specification before shipping.
  2. Level 2: on site, installation is inspected against drawings (labels, torque, cabling) before power-on.
  3. Level 3: each piece of equipment is started up and set up, usually by its manufacturer.
  4. Level 4: functional performance tests check each system on its own in all modes, including failures.
  5. Level 5: the Integrated Systems Test runs everything together under full simulated load, including real power failures.

Who uses it

Commissioning agents/authorities, design engineers, contractors, vendor engineers and the future operations team all take part; Cx engineering is a well-paid specialism.

Key takeaway

Get the operations team involved in commissioning: it is the best training they will ever get on how their site really behaves.

Going deeper

  • Commissioning starts at design: the CxA reviews the owner's project requirements and basis of design, writes commissioning into the specifications, and prepares test scripts long before equipment arrives.
  • Level 5 load banks are sized to the full design IT load and placed in the data halls so cooling is tested too; reactive load banks also test generators at realistic power factors.
  • Typical IST scenarios include utility loss and return, generator fail-to-start, UPS module failure, chiller trip with standby start, controller failure, and fire-alarm interfaces such as damper closure.
  • Hyperscale builds commission hall by hall and use prefabricated skids tested at the factory, moving more work into Level 1 and shortening on-site testing.
  • The handover package includes as-built drawings, O&M manuals, test results, a closed issues log, spare parts and training records; operations teams should refuse a site without them.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Skipping Level 5 because Level 4 passed; interactions between generators, UPSs and controls only appear when tested together.
  • Testing at low load; overheating and protection problems often appear only near design load.
  • Leaving the operations team out; they lose the best chance to learn how the site really behaves.

docs.title: Try it: Excerpt of a Level 5 IST test script (YAML)
docs.text:
ist_test:
  id: L5-07
  title: Loss of utility, full load
  preconditions:
    - Load banks at 100% design IT load (24 MW)
    - All UPS on line mode, generators in auto
  actions:
    - Open utility incomer breakers MV-1 and MV-2
  acceptance:
    - IT load uninterrupted (UPS bridges gap)
    - All generators on bus within 15 s
    - Cold-aisle temps stay below 27 C throughout
  restore: Return to utility after 60 min on generator
  result: PASS / FAIL with issues logged

docs.title: 6.10 Capacity Planning
docs.text:
Capacity planning means knowing how much power, cooling, space and network connectivity the site has, how much is used or promised, and when it will run out. Because new capacity takes months or years to build, planners must forecast demand early. They also keep safe margins so a failure or peak never overloads anything.

Hall 3 capacity at Kestrel Colo. The hall looks half empty by measured load, yet it is sold out by contract and policy.

Think of it like…

It is like managing seats on a plane: you track seats sold, seats actually filled, and seats that cannot be sold because a broken seat blocks the row.

Real-world example

Hall 3 at the fictional Kestrel Colo has 4.0 MW design IT capacity. Customers have contracted 3.4 MW but actually draw only 2.1 MW. Some racks sit in a row whose cooling is full, stranding 0.3 MW of power. With an 85% sales limit on design capacity (3.4 MW), Hall 3 is effectively sold out until the stranded 0.3 MW is recovered by upgrading cooling.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Record design capacity for power, cooling, space and network, respecting redundancy.
  2. Track contracted (reserved) and actual (measured) usage for each.
  3. Find stranded capacity, where one resource is left unusable because another has run out.
  4. Forecast growth from sales pipelines and trends; model 'what if' scenarios.
  5. Apply headroom rules and plan new builds or upgrades well before limits are reached.

Who uses it

Capacity planners, data centre managers, sales engineers and design engineers work on this; it links engineering to the commercial side.

Key takeaway

Always ask 'capacity of what, measured where?': design, contracted and actual load are very different numbers.

Going deeper

  • Track each resource separately (power at every level of the chain from utility and UPS to PDU, RPP and breaker, plus cooling, space, floor load and ports); real capacity is set by whichever runs out first.
  • Colocation customers often draw well below their contracted power for months or years, which tempts operators to oversell; that is safe only with good metering and enforced contract limits.
  • Redundancy halves usable capacity: in a 2N design each side should normally stay below 50% of its rating, often 40-45% for margin, so it can carry the whole load alone.
  • AI changes the maths: training clusters run close to nameplate and swing quickly between idle and full power, so the diversity factors used for enterprise IT do not apply.
  • Lead times drive the planning horizon: grid connections can take several years and large transformers, switchgear and generators often more than a year, so plans look three to five years ahead.
  • Stranded capacity is usually recovered by rebalancing A and B loads, adding in-row or rear-door cooling, moving racks between rows or replacing low-density legacy equipment.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Planning enterprise IT on nameplate power; it overstates typical draw, but for AI training assume near-nameplate.
  • Forgetting that each 2N side must carry the whole load; 60% on both sides means an overload after any failover.
  • Selling space before checking cooling and network capacity in that row; you create stranded capacity.

docs.title: Try it: Headroom calculation (Python)
docs.text:
design_mw, contracted_mw, actual_mw, stranded_mw = 4.0, 3.4, 2.1, 0.3
sell_limit = 0.85 * design_mw            # keep 15% headroom
sellable = max(0, sell_limit - contracted_mw - stranded_mw)
print(f"Utilisation of design: {actual_mw/design_mw:.0%}")   # 52%
print(f"Contracted ratio:      {contracted_mw/design_mw:.0%}")  # 85%
print(f"Still sellable:        {sellable:.2f} MW")            # 0.00 MW

docs.title: 6.11 Incident & Outage Management
docs.text:
An incident is anything that disrupts, or could disrupt, the service, from a single failed fan to a full site blackout. Incident management is the organised way to respond: spot it, rate how serious it is, fix it, keep everyone informed, and learn from it afterwards. Studying real outages is one of the best ways to understand what goes wrong in data centres.

The incident management cycle. The cycle closes only when corrective actions are complete, so the same failure cannot happen twice.

Think of it like…

It is like a fire brigade: a clear chain of command at the scene, a set way of working, and a full investigation afterwards so the same fire does not happen again.

Real-world example

At 03:12 a UPS at the fictional Harbourview DC transfers to bypass and an alarm fires. The shift lead declares a Severity 2 incident, becomes incident commander, opens a bridge call and notifies affected customers within 15 minutes. The vendor finds a failed control board; power is back on UPS by 07:40. A blameless review later finds the board had shown warning codes for weeks that nobody was trained to read, so training and alarm mapping are fixed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Detect: alarms, monitoring or a customer report reveal a problem.
  2. Assess and classify severity; appoint an incident commander and open a bridge or war room.
  3. Contain and restore service, following EOPs; communicate regularly to customers and management.
  4. Close the incident once stable, then perform root cause analysis.
  5. Hold a blameless post-incident review and track corrective actions to completion.

Who uses it

Everyone in operations takes part; incident managers, shift leads and customer-service teams lead communication; reliability engineers run RCAs.

Key takeaway

Uptime Institute surveys consistently find power is the leading cause of serious outages and that most human-error outages involve procedures not being followed or flawed processes.

Going deeper

  • Uptime Institute's annual outage analyses keep finding on-site power problems the leading cause of impactful outages, and a growing share of significant outages now cost more than US$100,000.
  • Incident roles follow the Incident Command System: an incident commander decides, an operations lead fixes, a communications lead updates customers and managers, and a scribe keeps the timeline.
  • Customer communication runs on a clock: first notice within a set time, often 15-30 minutes, updates at fixed intervals even without news, then preliminary and final RFO reports.
  • Root-cause work combines 5 whys, fishbone diagrams, fault trees and timelines rebuilt from EPMS and BMS logs; serious incidents usually have several contributing causes, not one.
  • Lithium-ion battery fires are a growing incident class, from Digital Realty Singapore in 2024 to South Korea's NIRS in 2025, driving battery-room separation and better suppression.
  • The OVHcloud fire made fire compartmentation, quick power isolation for firefighters and off-site backups standard questions in customer due diligence.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Fixing before communicating; customers and managers need early, regular updates even before the cause is known.
  • Stopping at 'human error'; ask why the system allowed the error, through procedures, training or design.
  • Leaving corrective actions untracked; repeat incidents follow when actions have no owner or deadline.

docs.title: 6.12 Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery Across Sites
docs.text:
Business continuity means keeping important services running when something goes badly wrong, such as a fire, flood, cyber attack or regional power cut. Disaster recovery (DR) is the technical part: copying data and systems to another site so they can be restarted there. Because even the best single building can fail, serious organisations plan for losing a whole site.

Choosing a DR pattern

Backup & restore Warm standby Active-active Typical RTO Hours to days Minutes to hours Near zero Typical RPO Since last backup Seconds to minutes Zero to seconds Second-site cost Low Medium High (full capacity) Complexity Low Medium High Typical use Archives, internal tools Business applications Payments, major web services

Faster recovery and less data loss cost more, so match the pattern to the business impact analysis.

Think of it like…

It is like keeping a spare house key at a friend's place across town: a better lock on your front door does not help if the house itself burns down.

Real-world example

Fictional payments firm Paywell runs its core system in a Tier III colocation site in Manchester and replicates data every few seconds to a second site in London, about 260 km away. Its business impact analysis sets a one-hour RTO and a five-minute RPO. Twice a year the team fails over to London for a weekend and measures how long it really takes. The first test took three hours because DNS changes and firewall rules had been forgotten, so the runbook was fixed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Run a business impact analysis to rank services and decide how much downtime and data loss each can tolerate.
  2. Set RTO and RPO targets per service and choose a DR pattern (backup and restore, warm standby or active-active) that meets them.
  3. Place the second site far enough away to avoid shared risks such as the same flood plain, substation or fault line.
  4. Replicate data and configuration, protect backups from tampering, and write step-by-step failover and failback runbooks.
  5. Test regularly, from tabletop exercises to full failovers, then fix the gaps and test again.

Who uses it

Business continuity managers, DR and infrastructure architects, site reliability engineers, data-centre operations managers and auditors working to ISO 22301 or financial rules such as DORA.

Key takeaway

Interview favourite: RTO is how long you can be down, RPO is how much data you can afford to lose, and both are business decisions before they are technical ones.

Going deeper

  • Light in fibre travels about 5 microseconds per kilometre one way, so synchronous replication, which waits for the remote write, is usually kept within roughly 100 km to avoid slowing every transaction.
  • Facility resilience (Tier levels, 2N power, N+1 cooling) protects against equipment failure inside one building; DR protects against losing the building, so mature organisations budget for both.
  • Cloud regions are split into availability zones a few kilometres to tens of kilometres apart for synchronous designs, while separate regions hundreds of kilometres apart cover regional disasters.
  • Ransomware changed DR design: replicas copy encrypted data within seconds, so organisations add immutable, delayed or offline copies and rehearse rebuilding from clean backups.
  • Dependencies sink failovers: DNS, identity services, certificates, licences, firewall rules and third-party APIs must all work at the DR site, so runbooks map every one.
  • Financial regulators now demand evidence: the EU's DORA requires tested ICT continuity and recovery plans, and supervisors expect documented results, not just written plans.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming RAID, 2N power or a Tier IV building is disaster recovery; they protect one site, not against losing it.
  • Putting the DR site on the same flood plain, substation or carrier route as production, so one event takes out both.
  • Never testing failover; untested plans usually miss DNS, credentials or licences, and the real RTO turns out several times longer.
  • Replicating without immutable copies, so ransomware or an accidental deletion reaches the DR site within seconds.

docs.title: Try it: Check DR test results against RTO/RPO targets (Python)
docs.text:
targets = {"payments": (60, 5), "email": (480, 60)}   # minutes: (RTO, RPO)
results = {"payments": (175, 2), "email": (300, 30)}  # measured in last DR test

for svc, (rto, rpo) in targets.items():
    took, lost = results[svc]
    ok = took <= rto and lost <= rpo
    print(f"{svc:9} RTO {took}/{rto} min  RPO {lost}/{rpo} min  -> {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}")

docs.title: 6.13 SLAs, Customer Service & Remote Hands
docs.text:
Colocation and managed data centres sell promises as well as space. A Service Level Agreement (SLA) is the contract that says how available the power and cooling will be, how fast staff will respond, and what money comes back if the promise is broken. Day to day, customers deal with the site through tickets, a web portal and on-site 'remote hands' staff.

A remote-hands ticket. The SLA clock starts when the ticket is logged and stops when the customer is told it is done.

Think of it like…

An SLA is like a parcel delivery guarantee: if your 'next-day' parcel arrives late, you get part of your money back, and the tracking page is the customer portal.

Real-world example

Fictional fintech PayLark rents 20 racks at Kestrel Colo with a 99.999% power-availability SLA and a 30-minute remote-hands response time. One night PayLark's engineer, 400 km away, raises a ticket asking for a server to be power-cycled. A technician does it in 12 minutes and attaches a photo. When a breaker fault later cuts one rack's A and B feeds for 9 minutes, the SLA is breached and PayLark receives a service credit worth 10% of that month's fee.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The contract defines what is promised (power, temperature, response times) and how it is measured.
  2. Customers request work and access through tickets or the portal.
  3. On-site staff perform remote-hands tasks, receive deliveries and escort visitors.
  4. Monitoring records SLA performance; breaches are reported with a reason-for-outage report.
  5. Credits are paid as defined, and repeat issues are reviewed with the customer.

Who uses it

Customer-service agents, account managers, remote-hands technicians and NOC staff work with SLAs every day; remote hands is a common first job in the industry.

Key takeaway

Read SLAs closely: a 'power' SLA often only counts when both A and B feeds fail, and credits are usually capped well below the customer's real losses.

Going deeper

  • Availability maths: 99.999% allows about 5.3 minutes of downtime a year, 99.99% about 53 minutes and 99.9% about 8.8 hours; check whether the SLA is measured monthly or yearly.
  • Service credits are typically tiered by how badly the target was missed, capped (often at one month's fees) and must be claimed by the customer within a deadline.
  • Environmental SLAs usually reference the ASHRAE recommended inlet range of 18-27 °C at defined sensor points; customers should ask where, and how often, temperature is measured.
  • Remote hands is commonly billed in 15- or 30-minute increments with a minimum charge, or as a monthly allowance; 'smart hands' covers more skilled tasks such as installs and troubleshooting.
  • A power SLA protects only correctly connected equipment: dual-corded devices on both feeds, total load low enough for one feed to carry it, and rack transfer switches for single-corded kit.
  • Customers also expect compliance evidence such as SOC 2 and ISO 27001 reports, site audits and honest, prompt RFOs; good service keeps customers through bad incidents.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming a 99.999% SLA means no outage; it is a promise of credit, not a guarantee of uptime.
  • Loading A and B feeds so their combined draw exceeds one feed's rating; if one feed fails, the other trips too.
  • Ignoring exclusions; announced maintenance and customer-caused faults usually do not count toward the SLA.

docs.title: Try it: Convert an availability SLA into allowed downtime (Python)
docs.text:
for sla in (99.9, 99.99, 99.999):
    minutes = (1 - sla/100) * 365 * 24 * 60
    print(f"{sla}% -> {minutes:,.1f} min/year, {minutes/12:,.2f} min/month")
# 99.9%   -> 525.6 min/year
# 99.99%  ->  52.6 min/year
# 99.999% ->   5.3 min/year

docs.title: 6.14 Staffing, Shift Patterns & Skills
docs.text:
Keeping skilled people on site around the clock is one of the hardest parts of running a data centre. Teams work rotating shifts so someone is always there, with enough people to handle a serious failure at 3 a.m. The industry is short of trained staff, so training, knowledge sharing and automation all matter.

Common 12-hour shift patterns

4-on-4-off DuPont Panama (2-2-3) Teams needed 4 4 4 Cycle length 8 days 4 weeks 2 weeks Long break 4 days every cycle 7 days once per cycle Every other weekend off Average hours about 42 a week about 42 a week about 42 a week Main drawback Weekends rotate Tough run of nights Short breaks between blocks

All three average about 42 hours a week with four teams; they differ in how rest days are grouped.

Think of it like…

It is like a lifeboat crew: there must always be enough trained people on duty to launch the boat, not just someone to answer the phone.

Real-world example

The fictional Fernhill DC needs two engineers on site at all times. Covering one 24/7 seat takes 8,760 hours a year, and one engineer works about 1,800 hours after leave and training, so each seat needs about five people. Fernhill runs four teams on a 12-hour rotation, plus a day-shift maintenance team. New hires shadow experienced staff for six weeks and must pass a competency sign-off on every EOP before working alone.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide the minimum number and skills of people needed on site at every hour, based on the worst credible failure.
  2. Choose a shift pattern (e.g. 12-hour rotations) and calculate how many people it takes, including leave and training.
  3. Train staff with a competency matrix, shadowing and supervised drills.
  4. Back up shifts with an on-call rota and vendor support contracts.
  5. Review fatigue, turnover and lessons from incidents; use automation to reduce routine workload.

Who uses it

Operations managers, HR and training teams design staffing; every technician and engineer works within it.

Key takeaway

Minimum staffing must be based on what is needed to respond to a major failure, not on normal quiet nights.

Going deeper

  • Staffing factor: one 24/7 seat needs 8,760 hours a year; after leave, training and sickness a person works about 1,700-1,900 hours, so each seat needs roughly five people.
  • Set minimum staffing from credible worst cases, such as a night-time utility failure with a generator that fails to start, and list the tasks needed in the first 15-30 minutes.
  • Microsoft's review of the August 2023 Australia East incident found the night shift too small to restart tripped chillers manually in time, and the company increased night staffing afterwards.
  • Error rates rise on night shifts and after several consecutive 12-hour shifts, so limit runs of nights, avoid quick returns and schedule critical work for well-rested teams.
  • Uptime Institute surveys report that most operators struggle to hire or keep qualified staff; pipelines include apprenticeships, military veterans and vendor academies.
  • Uptime's Tier Certification of Operational Sustainability scores staffing and organisation, maintenance, training and planning, linking people practices to a recognised certificate.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Staffing for quiet nights; a major failure needs more hands than routine monitoring.
  • Counting one person per seat; leave, training and sickness mean about five people per 24/7 role.
  • Letting experienced staff leave without capturing their knowledge; record it in procedures and shadowing plans.

docs.title: Try it: How many people does one 24/7 seat need? (Python)
docs.text:
hours_per_year = 365 * 24          # 8,760
worked_per_person = 52*42 - 25*12 - 5*12   # 42 h/week minus leave & training days (12 h shifts)
print(worked_per_person)                       # 1,824 h
print(round(hours_per_year / worked_per_person, 1), 'people per 24/7 seat')   # ~4.8

docs.title: 6.15 Health & Safety in the Data Centre
docs.text:
Data centres contain high-voltage electricity, large batteries, heavy equipment, loud generators and fuel, so safety rules come first. Workers isolate energy before touching equipment, use permits for risky work and wear the right protective equipment. Safety is part of every procedure, not an add-on.

Hierarchy of controls. Start at the top: PPE is the last line of defence, not the first.

Think of it like…

Safety rules are like seatbelts: they feel slow until the one day they save your life.

Real-world example

Technician Ravi at the fictional Lakeside DC must replace a fan in a CRAH unit. He gets a permit-to-work, switches off the unit's isolator, fits his personal padlock and tag, and tests for zero voltage with a meter he first checks on a known live source. Only then does he open the panel. At the end he removes his lock, the shift lead closes the permit, and the unit is restarted following the SOP.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Assess risks and plan the job; write or check the RAMS (risk assessment and method statement).
  2. Obtain a permit-to-work for higher-risk tasks (electrical, hot work, confined space, height).
  3. Isolate and lock out energy sources, then test to prove they are dead.
  4. Wear correct PPE (arc-rated clothing, eye and hearing protection, safety boots, gloves).
  5. Do the work, remove locks only when safe, close the permit and report any near misses.

Who uses it

Everyone on site, especially engineers, technicians and contractors; health and safety managers set the rules and audit them.

Key takeaway

Never work on live electrical equipment if it can be de-energised; energised work is the rare exception, needs special justification and an energised work permit.

Going deeper

  • Test before touch: prove the voltage tester on a known live source, test the isolated circuit phase to phase and phase to earth, then re-prove the tester.
  • Group lockout: when several people work on one isolation, the isolation keys go into a lock box and each worker fits a personal lock to the box until their part is done.
  • Lithium-ion battery rooms need off-gas detection, thermal-runaway mitigation, separation from data halls and fire-service plans; NFPA 855 and UL 9540A test data guide the design.
  • AI-era hazards include 1-1.5 tonne racks that need powered movers and planned routes, and liquid cooling that adds pressurised coolant, glycol handling and slip risks.
  • Leading indicators such as near-miss reports, safety observations and toolbox talks predict accidents better than lagging injury rates; healthy sites report many near misses.
  • UK noise rules require hearing protection to be available from 80 dB(A) daily exposure and worn from 85 dB(A); generator yards and fan walls can exceed these levels.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Trusting a switch position or an 'off' label; always test for absence of voltage before touching.
  • Removing someone else's lock; only the person who fitted it may remove it, except under a controlled lock-removal procedure.
  • Treating near misses as luck; report them so the cause is fixed before someone is hurt.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Power Infrastructure
docs.text: Power is the lifeblood of every data centre: if it stops for even a fraction of a second, servers crash. This chapter follows electricity from the grid and on-site substation through transformers, switchgear, UPS systems, batteries and generators all the way to the power supply inside each server. It explains redundancy, the huge new demands of AI racks, how sites connect to strained grids and buy nuclear power, and the safety rules that keep technicians alive.

docs.title: 2.1 Electricity Basics for Data Centres
docs.text:
Electricity is the flow of tiny charged particles through a wire, and a data centre is basically a machine that turns huge amounts of it into computing (and heat). Voltage is the 'push', current is the 'flow', and power is how much work they do together each second. A few simple formulas let you work out how big every cable, breaker and generator needs to be.

Sizing a rack circuit, step by step. Worked example: a 17.5 kW rack at 415 V three-phase and PF 0.95 needs a 32 A circuit.

Think of it like…

Think of a garden hose: voltage is the water pressure, current is how many litres flow per second, and power is how hard the jet can push a toy boat across the pond.

Real-world example

Priya, a new technician at the fictional Northgate Data, is asked whether a 415 V three-phase, 32 A rack feed can carry a 20 kW AI server rack. She calculates √3 × 415 × 32 × 0.95 ≈ 21.9 kW at full rating. Because circuits should normally run at no more than 80% of their rating, the safe limit is about 17.5 kW, so she flags that the rack needs two feeds or a 63 A circuit.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Voltage (V) pushes current (A) through a circuit; the electrical resistance or load decides how much current flows.
  2. Real power in watts (W) does useful work; apparent power in volt-amperes (VA) is what the cables and transformers must carry.
  3. Power factor (PF) = W ÷ VA; modern server power supplies have a PF close to 1.0.
  4. Most data-centre power is three-phase AC, which delivers more power per copper conductor than single-phase.
  5. Electronics turn AC into DC inside their power supplies, creating harmonics that the electrical design must cope with.
  6. Every watt the IT equipment uses ends up as heat that the cooling system must remove.

Who uses it

Electrical engineers, critical facilities technicians, data-centre designers and capacity planners use these basics every day.

Key takeaway

Memorise the three-phase power formula P = √3 × V(line-to-line) × I × PF; it appears in almost every data-centre interview and sizing question.

Going deeper

  • Three-phase power is P = √3 × V(line-to-line) × I × PF, single-phase is P = V × I × PF; at 415 V each ampere of three-phase current carries about 0.72 kW at unity PF.
  • Cable and breaker sizing considers continuous current, ambient temperature, cable grouping, voltage drop and prospective fault current, using tables in IEC 60364-5-52 or NEC Article 310.
  • Switch-mode power supplies draw current in pulses, creating odd harmonics; triplen harmonics (3rd, 9th, 15th) add up in the neutral, which can then carry more current than a phase.
  • Server power supplies use active power-factor correction to meet harmonic limits such as IEC 61000-3-2, so modern IT loads distort the supply far less than early-2000s equipment.
  • Test instruments carry IEC 61010 measurement categories (CAT II-IV) for transient energy; switchboard work needs CAT III or CAT IV meters, never cheap household testers.
  • Engineers start every task at the single-line diagram, which shows every source that can feed a point, including UPS batteries and generator backfeeds that may keep a circuit live.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Forgetting power factor: sizing in kW but buying a UPS rated in kVA can leave it short of real capacity.
  • Loading a breaker to 100% continuously: plan for 80% unless the assembly is specifically rated for 100% continuous duty.
  • Assuming an open breaker means a dead circuit: always test for absence of voltage, because other sources may backfeed.

docs.title: 2.2 The Utility Grid & Substations
docs.text:
Power stations make electricity far away, and the grid carries it at very high voltage over long distances, then steps it down in substations before it reaches users. Big data centres need so much power that they often have their own substation on site, fed by one or more high-voltage lines. Getting that connection is now one of the hardest and slowest parts of building a data centre.

From power station to building. Voltage is stepped down at each tier; big campuses connect high up the chain with their own substation.

Think of it like…

The grid is like a river system: huge rivers (transmission lines) carry water across the country, and dams and locks (substations) lower the level so smaller canals can deliver it to each town.

Real-world example

The fictional Riverbend Cloud campus plans 300 MW of IT load. The local utility agrees to build two 230 kV lines from different directions into a new on-site substation with three 100 MVA transformers stepping down to 34.5 kV. Each data hall gets two medium-voltage feeds, so the loss of one line or one transformer does not stop the campus. The connection takes four years, longer than building the halls themselves.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Power stations generate electricity, which is stepped up to high voltage (for example 132-400 kV) for efficient long-distance transmission.
  2. Transmission lines carry power to grid substations, where transformers step it down to sub-transmission or distribution voltages.
  3. Large campuses take power directly at high voltage into an on-site substation owned by the utility or the operator.
  4. Two independent utility feeds from different substations or lines protect against a single line failure.
  5. Medium-voltage cables then distribute power around the campus to each building's transformers and switchgear.

Who uses it

Utility engineers, grid planners, data-centre power engineers and site-selection teams work on grid connections and substations.

Key takeaway

Know the voltage classes: low voltage up to 1 kV AC, medium voltage roughly 1-35 kV, high voltage above that (exact boundaries differ by country and standard).

Going deeper

  • Grids transmit at high voltage because losses scale with current squared: 100 MW at 400 kV needs about 144 A per phase, versus about 5,250 A at 11 kV.
  • Utilities plan to N-1 security, so the network survives losing any single line or transformer; large customers often fund extra circuits to obtain genuinely dual supplies.
  • Large campuses commonly take 115-345 kV in North America or 110-400 kV in Europe into a dedicated substation, then distribute on site at medium voltage such as 33 kV or 34.5 kV.
  • Large power transformers are custom-built, can weigh over 100 tonnes and have had multi-year lead times, so spares and standardised designs reduce restoration risk.
  • Grid codes increasingly treat very large data-centre loads like power plants, requiring voltage and frequency ride-through, ramp-rate limits and data sharing with the grid operator.
  • Protection relays, often communicating over IEC 61850, clear grid faults in tens of milliseconds; the data centre's UPS must still ride through the voltage dip a remote fault causes.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming two incoming cables are independent: check they come from different substations along different routes.
  • Underestimating connection timelines: grid studies, upgrades and transformer deliveries can take longer than building the halls.
  • Expecting the utility to guarantee uptime: outages and voltage dips are normal grid events, which is why UPS and generators exist.

docs.title: Try it: Why grids use high voltage: line current for the same 100 MW

import math
power_w = 100e6
for kv in (11, 33, 132, 400):
    amps = power_w / (math.sqrt(3) * kv * 1000)
    print(f"{kv:>4} kV -> {amps:,.0f} A per phase")
# Higher voltage = less current = thinner cables and lower losses (I²R)

docs.title: 2.3 Medium & Low-Voltage Distribution
docs.text:
Inside the site, power travels at medium voltage to transformers near each building, which step it down to the low voltage that equipment uses. Switchgear and circuit breakers act as giant, smart switches and fuses that can turn sections on or off and cut power instantly if something goes wrong. This is the 'grey space' backbone that everything else hangs from.

Medium voltage down to the rack. Breakers get smaller at every stage, and only the one nearest a fault should trip.

Think of it like…

It is like a home's fuse box scaled up a thousand times: one main switch feeding many smaller switches, each protecting one branch of the house.

Real-world example

At the fictional Lakeside DC in Frankfurt, two 20 kV ring main units feed four 2,500 kVA cast-resin transformers that step down to 400 V. Each transformer feeds a main low-voltage switchboard with air circuit breakers. During a fault on one outgoing cable, the nearest MCCB trips within milliseconds while the upstream breakers stay closed, so only one PDU loses power and its racks switch to their B feed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Medium-voltage cables bring power to ring main units or MV switchgear at each building.
  2. Transformers step the voltage down to low voltage, for example 480 V in the US or 400 V in Europe.
  3. Main LV switchboards with air circuit breakers distribute power to UPS systems, cooling plant and building services.
  4. Protection relays and breaker trip units detect overloads and short circuits and open the right breaker.
  5. A coordination study makes sure the breaker nearest a fault trips first (selectivity), limiting the outage.

Who uses it

Electrical engineers, switchgear technicians, commissioning agents and critical facilities engineers design, test and maintain this equipment.

Key takeaway

Learn the common voltages: US 480/277 V and 208/120 V, Europe 400/230 V, and 415/240 V used by many hyperscale designs.

Going deeper

  • Transformer impedance, often around 5-6% for large distribution units, limits fault current; a lower-impedance or larger transformer raises the kA rating needed downstream.
  • Selective coordination uses time-current curves: downstream devices trip faster, upstream ones wait slightly longer, and a study checks every pair for overlaps across the system.
  • Drawout air circuit breakers can be racked to test or disconnected positions, giving a visible isolation point and allowing quick replacement from a spare.
  • Main-tie-main boards let either of two transformers feed both bus sections through a tie breaker, so one transformer can be maintained while loads stay energised.
  • Equipment must be rated for the prospective short-circuit current at its location, calculated with IEC 60909 or IEEE methods and updated whenever the system changes.
  • EU Ecodesign rules (Regulation 548/2014, amended by 2019/1783) set minimum efficiency levels for power transformers, pushing designs toward lower-loss cores and windings.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Fitting a bigger transformer without rechecking fault levels: downstream breakers may no longer interrupt faults safely.
  • Changing trip settings without a coordination study, so a minor rack fault can trip a main board.
  • Installing oil-filled transformers indoors without fire separation and oil containment.

docs.title: 2.4 Uninterruptible Power Supplies (UPS)
docs.text:
A UPS sits between the mains supply and the IT equipment and keeps power flowing, without even a flicker, when the grid fails. It uses stored energy (usually batteries, sometimes a spinning flywheel) to bridge the gap until generators start, typically in 10-15 seconds. Many UPS designs also clean up the power, removing spikes, dips and noise.

The three UPS types (IEC 62040-3)

Standby (VFD) Line-interactive (VI) Double conversion (VFI) Normal path Mains straight to load Mains via regulating transformer Rectifier → DC → inverter On mains failure Brief transfer (ms) Brief transfer (ms) Zero break Conditioning Minimal Voltage regulation Full isolation from mains Typical size Under a few kVA Small, rack-mount 10 kVA to multi-MW Typical use Home and desktop Branch office, edge rack Data halls

Only double conversion gives zero transfer time and full isolation, which is why data halls use it.

Think of it like…

A UPS is like a bridge over a river: the grid is the road on one bank, the generator the road on the other, and the UPS lets traffic cross the gap without stopping.

Real-world example

At the fictional Meadowbank colo, a storm causes a utility outage at 2:14 a.m. The double-conversion UPS instantly switches to battery with zero break, carrying 1.2 MW. The generators start in 9 seconds, the ATS transfers after a short stabilisation delay, and the UPS returns to normal operation drawing from the generators; the batteries used about 40 seconds of their 8-minute autonomy.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Normal mode: incoming AC is converted (rectified) to DC, which charges the batteries and feeds an inverter.
  2. The inverter creates clean new AC for the IT load, isolating it from grid disturbances (double conversion).
  3. If the input fails, the batteries already connected to the DC bus keep the inverter running with no break.
  4. When generators or the grid return, the rectifier takes over and recharges the batteries.
  5. If the UPS itself has a problem, a static bypass switches the load straight to the input supply in milliseconds.

Who uses it

Critical facilities engineers, UPS field service engineers and electrical designers specify, maintain and test UPS systems.

Key takeaway

Know the IEC 62040-3 classes: VFI (double-conversion online), VI (line-interactive) and VFD (standby/offline).

Going deeper

  • IEC 62040-3 codes such as VFI-SS-111 describe input dependency (VFI, VI or VFD), output waveform in normal and battery modes, and dynamic output performance during load and mode changes.
  • IT power supplies ride through very short interruptions: the ITI (CBEMA) curve expects equipment to tolerate total loss of voltage for about 20 ms, far shorter than a generator start.
  • Modern transformerless double-conversion modules reach roughly 96-97% efficiency, while eco or energy-saver modes reach about 99% by running on bypass with the inverter ready to take over.
  • UPS systems are sized for the critical load plus redundancy, with battery autonomy usually 5-10 minutes at full load and margin for end-of-life battery capacity.
  • An external maintenance bypass wrapped around the whole UPS system is essential for concurrent maintainability, letting engineers isolate every module without dropping load.
  • Some hyperscale designs replace central UPS with in-rack battery backup units or distributed UPS, accepting shorter runtimes in exchange for fewer conversion losses.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming every UPS is double conversion: small standby and line-interactive units have a transfer gap some equipment cannot tolerate.
  • Operating a maintenance bypass out of sequence: one wrong step can drop the load, so always follow the MOP.
  • Loading a redundant module group beyond its N capacity, so one module failure overloads the rest.

docs.title: 2.5 Batteries & Energy Storage
docs.text:
Batteries are the energy store behind most UPS systems, holding enough power for a few minutes until generators take over. Older sites use lead-acid batteries; newer ones increasingly use lithium-ion, which is smaller, lighter and lasts longer but needs careful fire-risk management. Batteries are also one of the most common causes of UPS failures, so they are watched closely.

UPS battery chemistries

VRLA lead-acid Lithium-ion LFP Lithium-ion NMC Design life ~5-10 years ~15 years ~10-15 years Footprint Largest, heaviest Much smaller, lighter Smallest, lightest Thermal runaway Low (vents hydrogen) Lower than NMC Highest of the three Monitoring Add-on block monitoring Built-in BMS Built-in BMS Trend Large installed base Increasingly the default Less common in new UPS

Lithium saves space and lasts longer, but every chemistry needs monitoring and fire-code compliance.

Think of it like…

A UPS battery string is like a car's spare fuel can: you hope never to need it, but you check it regularly, because finding it empty in an emergency is the worst moment to learn.

Real-world example

The fictional Orchard Data replaces 640 VRLA lead-acid blocks with lithium iron phosphate cabinets. The battery room footprint drops by about 60%, and the design life rises from about 5 years to 15. The new system has a battery management system that reports every cell's voltage and temperature, and the room is fitted with gas detection and protection designed to NFPA 855.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Batteries are wired in series 'strings' to reach the UPS DC bus voltage, often several hundred volts.
  2. Several strings in parallel provide the energy needed for the required runtime and add redundancy.
  3. Monitoring systems track voltage, internal resistance and temperature of each block or cell.
  4. Temperature control matters: lead-acid life roughly halves for every 8-10 °C above 25 °C.
  5. Fire codes set rules on spacing, ventilation, detection and suppression for large battery systems.

Who uses it

Critical facilities technicians, battery service engineers, fire-safety engineers and UPS specialists work with data-centre batteries.

Key takeaway

Remember the chemistry trade-off: LFP is safer and longer-lasting, NMC is more energy-dense; both need thermal-runaway protection.

Going deeper

  • Lead-acid UPS batteries are sized from makers' constant-power discharge tables to an end voltage, typically about 1.67-1.75 V per cell for short UPS runtimes.
  • Available capacity depends on discharge rate and temperature: a battery delivers less energy at a five-minute rate than at a ten-hour rate, so amp-hour ratings alone mislead.
  • Lead-acid life falls sharply with heat; a common rule is about half the life lost for every 8-10 °C sustained above 25 °C, so battery rooms are kept cool.
  • Lithium systems carry a built-in BMS, and codes such as NFPA 855 and the International Fire Code set quantity limits, separation and detection, informed by UL 9540A test results.
  • Internal resistance (ohmic) trending spots weakening blocks between discharge tests; a value rising well above its baseline triggers investigation or replacement.
  • Strings are normally replaced as a set near 80% capacity, because mixing new and aged blocks causes imbalance and early failures.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Confusing a lithium battery's BMS with the building management system: same acronym, completely different jobs.
  • Judging health by float voltage alone: a block can look normal yet fail under load; trend resistance and discharge test.
  • Letting battery rooms run warm to save cooling energy, which shortens lead-acid life dramatically.

docs.title: Try it: Rough UPS battery runtime estimate
docs.text:
load_kw = 800          # IT load on the UPS
inverter_eff = 0.95
usable_kwh = 120       # usable battery energy at this discharge rate
ageing_margin = 0.8    # plan for end-of-life capacity

minutes = usable_kwh * ageing_margin / (load_kw / inverter_eff) * 60
print(f"Estimated runtime: {minutes:.1f} minutes")
# Real sizing uses the maker's constant-power discharge tables

docs.title: 2.6 Generators, Fuel & Transfer Switching
docs.text:
Standby generators are big engines, usually diesel, that make electricity when the grid fails and can run for days if fuel is delivered. Transfer switches decide which source feeds the building and move the load between them automatically. Together with the UPS, they make sure a utility outage never reaches the servers.

A utility outage, second by second. The UPS covers the first seconds; generators carry the site until the grid is stable again.

Think of it like…

If the UPS is a sprinter that covers the first few seconds, the generator is the marathon runner who takes over and keeps going as long as you keep feeding it.

Real-world example

The fictional Granite Peak data centre has eight 2.5 MW diesel generators in N+1 with 48 hours of fuel on site. During a monthly test, the generators start, synchronise on the paralleling switchgear and carry the building for an hour. A fuel polishing system cleans the 200,000 litres of stored diesel, and an annual load-bank test runs each engine at full load for four hours to prevent wet stacking.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The ATS or switchgear controls detect a utility failure or out-of-tolerance voltage.
  2. Generators receive a start signal and reach speed and voltage, typically within about 10 seconds.
  3. In paralleled systems, generators synchronise onto a common bus before taking load.
  4. Transfer switches move the load to generator power; the UPS bridges the gap from batteries.
  5. When the utility is stable again, the load transfers back and generators cool down before stopping.

Who uses it

Generator technicians, critical facilities engineers, fuel suppliers and environmental permit specialists work on standby power.

Key takeaway

Know the ratings: emergency standby, prime and continuous under ISO 8528-1, and that data-centre ratings allow unlimited hours at a set average load when the grid is down.

Going deeper

  • NFPA 110 classifies emergency power systems by Type (seconds to restore power, e.g. Type 10) and Class (hours of fuel at rated load, e.g. Class 48), common language in US specifications.
  • On-site fuel autonomy targets commonly range from 24 to 72 hours, backed by priority refuelling contracts with more than one supplier for long grid outages.
  • Running diesels lightly loaded causes wet stacking, unburnt fuel building up in the exhaust; testing at meaningful load and annual load-bank runs prevent it.
  • ISO 8528-5 performance classes (G1-G4) set how far voltage and frequency may deviate during load steps; data-centre specifications usually call for the tighter classes.
  • Large campuses parallel generators onto MV buses such as 11 kV or 13.8 kV to share load, add redundancy and maintain one machine while others run.
  • Air permits often cap annual testing hours and set emission limits; HVO fuel and gas engines are adopted partly to cut emissions and local opposition.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Testing generators without load: no-load runs prove little and cause wet stacking; use building load or load banks.
  • Neglecting fuel quality: contaminated diesel is a classic cause of generator failure during long outages.
  • Forgetting the mechanical plant: if cooling is not on generator-backed power, IT overheats even though servers stay powered.

docs.title: Try it: Generator fuel burn and on-site autonomy
docs.text:
gens = 8
load_kw_each = 1800        # average load per running generator
litres_per_kwh = 0.27      # rough diesel figure near full load; check the datasheet
stored_litres = 200_000

burn_l_per_h = gens * load_kw_each * litres_per_kwh
hours = stored_litres / burn_l_per_h
print(f"Burn: {burn_l_per_h:,.0f} L/h, autonomy: {hours:.0f} hours")

docs.title: 2.7 Power Distribution to the Rack
docs.text:
After the UPS, power still has to reach hundreds of racks and thousands of servers. It travels through floor-standing power distribution units, panels or overhead busbars, then flexible cables ('whips') into the power strips inside each rack. Most servers have two power supplies plugged into two separate feeds, A and B, so losing one feed does not switch them off.

A and B feeds to a dual-corded server. Either path alone can carry the server, so one side can be maintained or fail without downtime.

Think of it like…

It is like a city's water mains: big pipes under the main road (busway), smaller pipes down each street (whips) and finally the taps in each kitchen (rack PDU outlets).

Real-world example

At the fictional Bluewater Colo, each row has two overhead busways, one from UPS A and one from UPS B. When a customer moves in, a technician clicks a plug-in tap-off unit onto each busway and drops a 32 A three-phase whip into the rack. Each rack has two switched, metered rack PDUs, and every dual-corded server plugs one supply into each, so a busway shutdown for maintenance causes no downtime.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. UPS output feeds floor PDUs (often with a transformer) or overhead busway running along each row.
  2. Remote power panels or busway tap-off boxes provide individually protected circuits for each rack.
  3. A whip (flexible cable with an industrial connector) runs from the breaker to the rack.
  4. Rack PDUs distribute power to IEC C13 or C19 outlets and can meter or switch each one.
  5. Dual-corded servers draw from both A and B rack PDUs, sharing the load and surviving the loss of either.

Who uses it

Data-centre technicians, installation electricians, colocation customer engineers and capacity planners handle rack power daily.

Key takeaway

Size A/B pairs so either feed alone can carry the whole rack within its 80% limit, which means about 40% per side in normal running.

Going deeper

  • Typical rack feed sizes: 230 V 32 A single-phase ≈ 7.4 kVA; 400 V 32 A three-phase ≈ 22 kVA; 208 V 30 A three-phase ≈ 10.8 kVA, all before the 80% continuous derating.
  • Each feed of an A/B pair normally carries half the rack but must carry it all alone, so with the 80% rule each side is planned at no more than about 40% in normal running.
  • Busway tap-off boxes carry their own breakers and often metering, and many systems allow them to be added while the busway stays live, speeding changes.
  • Intelligent rack PDUs report inlet, phase or outlet power over SNMP, Modbus or web APIs into DCIM, supporting capacity planning, customer billing and remote power cycling.
  • Denser racks move to 415 V or 480 V three-phase feeds and 60-63 A circuits, or to OCP-style power shelves feeding a DC busbar instead of many individual cords.
  • US floor PDUs often step 480 V down to 208/120 V; distributing at 415/240 V removes that transformer stage and its losses.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Plugging both power supplies into the same rack PDU: the server then has no feed redundancy at all.
  • Loading each side of an A/B pair above about 40%: if one feed fails, the survivor exceeds its limit and may trip.
  • Ignoring phase balance on three-phase rack PDUs, which strands capacity on one phase while another overloads.

docs.title: Try it: Check an A/B rack pair stays safe if one side fails
docs.text:
rack_load_kw = 14.0
pdu_capacity_kw = 22.0     # e.g. 400 V, 32 A three-phase
safe_limit = pdu_capacity_kw * 0.8

normal_each = rack_load_kw / 2
print(f"Normal: {normal_each:.1f} kW per side")
print("One side fails ->", rack_load_kw, "kW on survivor;",
      "OK" if rack_load_kw <= safe_limit else "OVERLOAD RISK")

docs.title: 2.8 Power Redundancy Architectures
docs.text:
Redundancy means having more equipment or more paths than you strictly need, so a breakdown or a planned repair does not stop the servers. Designers describe it with simple codes such as N, N+1 and 2N, where N is the amount needed to carry the load. More redundancy means higher reliability but also higher cost and more equipment sitting partly idle.

Three ways to protect a 3 MW load

N+1 (4 × 1 MW) 2N (2 × 3 MW) Distributed 4N/3 Installed UPS 4 MW 6 MW 4 MW Max normal loading 75% 50% 75% per system Survives One module failure Loss of a whole system Loss of any one system Separate paths No, single path Yes, A and B Yes, spread over four Relative cost Lowest Highest Medium

More installed capacity buys more resilience but lowers normal loading and raises cost.

Think of it like…

A family with three people and three umbrellas is N; keep one spare umbrella and you are N+1; give everyone two complete sets in two different cupboards and you are 2N.

Real-world example

The fictional Summit Hosting needs 3 MW of UPS capacity. With N+1 it installs four 1 MW modules on one system. A bank customer demands 2N, so Summit builds two fully separate 3 MW systems (A and B), using 6 MW of UPS for 3 MW of load. For a large AI hall it instead chooses distributed redundancy 4N/3: four 1 MW systems each loaded to 750 kW, so any one can fail and the other three absorb its load.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Work out N: the capacity needed to carry the full design IT load.
  2. Choose spare components (N+1, N+2) to survive equipment failure or maintenance on one unit.
  3. Choose spare paths (2N, distributed redundant) to survive failure of a whole system, switchboard or cable.
  4. Check concurrent maintainability: every component can be shut down for maintenance without dropping IT load.
  5. Check fault tolerance (for Tier IV): any single failure is automatically isolated without affecting IT.

Who uses it

Data-centre designers, reliability engineers, Uptime Institute accredited professionals and colocation sales engineers use these terms constantly.

Key takeaway

N+1 adds spare components; 2N duplicates the whole path; a design can be N+1 on generators but 2N on UPS, so always ask 'redundant for which system?'.

Going deeper

  • Notation applies per subsystem: a site might have dual utility feeds, N+1 generators, 2N UPS and N+1 chillers, and its overall resilience is limited by the weakest of them.
  • Distributed redundant schemes (3N/2, 4N/3) run each system more heavily than 2N, saving cost and losses, but need careful load placement so a failure redistributes as intended.
  • Block-redundant 'catcher' designs use static or automatic transfer switches to move a failed block's load onto a shared reserve system, popular in large colocation halls.
  • Reliability engineers use reliability block diagrams, FMEA and fault-tree analysis to find single points of failure and common-cause risks before anything is built.
  • Concurrent maintainability needs every component and path to be removable for planned work; fault tolerance also needs automatic response to failures and physical compartmentalisation.
  • Redundancy has costs beyond capital: lower normal loading reduces efficiency, and more complex switching creates more chances for operator error.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling a design 2N when both systems share a switchboard, control system or fuel supply.
  • Letting load grow until 'N+1' silently becomes N, because the spare unit is now needed to carry the load.
  • Assuming more redundancy is always better: complex switching adds failure modes and operator-error risk.

    "2N (2 systems of 3)": (6, 3),
    "Distributed 4N/3": (4, 3),
    "Distributed 3N/2": (3, 2),
}
for name, (installed, usable) in schemes.items():
    print(f"{name:24} installed {installed*unit_mw:.0f} MW, usable {usable*unit_mw:.0f} MW, "
          f"max normal loading {usable/installed:.0%}")

docs.title: 2.9 Power Density & AI-Era Power
docs.text:
AI servers packed with GPUs draw far more power per rack than ordinary servers, so power systems are being redesigned around them. A traditional rack might use 5-10 kW; a modern AI rack can use well over 100 kW, and future racks are planned near 1 MW. AI training also makes power demand jump up and down very quickly, which stresses UPS systems, generators and the grid.

Power per rack, then and next. AI pushed rack power up more than tenfold in a few years, and vendors now target 1 MW racks.

Think of it like…

Moving from normal racks to AI racks is like replacing a street of houses with a row of steelworks: the same street now needs thicker cables, bigger substations and a way to handle sudden surges.

Real-world example

The fictional Vantage Ridge AI campus plans halls of liquid-cooled racks drawing about 130 kW each. A 1,000-rack hall needs 130 MW of IT power, more than an entire traditional campus. During training, all GPUs pause together at checkpoints, so hall load can swing by tens of megawatts within a second. The design team adds rack-level energy storage and asks the GPU software team to enable power-smoothing settings.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Higher rack power means much higher current, so designers raise voltage to keep cable sizes manageable.
  2. Inside racks, power shelves convert AC to around 48-54 V DC busbars feeding server trays.
  3. Next-generation designs move AC-to-DC conversion out of the rack into sidecars or the facility (±400 V or 800 V DC).
  4. Energy storage at rack, row or facility level smooths sub-second AI load swings.
  5. Liquid cooling is required because air cannot remove heat at 100 kW+ per rack (see the cooling chapter).

Who uses it

AI infrastructure architects, hyperscale power engineers, GPU cluster operators and equipment vendors work on high-density power.

Key takeaway

Be ready to explain why voltage rises as density rises: for the same power, doubling voltage halves current, and cable losses fall to a quarter.

Going deeper

  • Current scales with power: a 130 kW rack at 415 V three-phase draws about 180 A at unity power factor, far beyond one 32 A or 63 A feed, so racks take several feeds or busway connections.
  • NVIDIA says its 800 V DC architecture supports racks from about 100 kW to over 1 MW, with full-scale production aligned to its Kyber rack-scale systems in 2027.
  • At 54 V a 1 MW rack would need roughly 18,500 A of busbar current, so conversion moves to sidecar racks or facility-level DC to cut copper and conversion stages.
  • Synchronised GPU work causes large, fast power swings at job starts and checkpoints; mitigations include rack energy storage, software ramp controls and GPU power caps.
  • OCP's Mt Diablo work, backed by Meta, Microsoft and Google, moves power conversion into a separate ±400 V DC sidecar so the IT rack holds more accelerators.
  • Higher-voltage DC brings new safety demands: DC arcs have no natural current zero to extinguish them, so breakers, connectors and training must be specified for DC faults.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Planning AI halls on average density: a few 130 kW racks beside 10 kW racks need point capacity, not averages.
  • Ignoring load dynamics: UPS, generators and the grid connection must handle rapid swings, not just peak kW.
  • Assuming 800 V DC is plug-and-play today: it is emerging, with standards and products still maturing.

docs.title: 2.10 Grounding, Bonding & Surge Protection
docs.text:
Grounding (earthing) connects the electrical system to the earth, and bonding connects all metal parts together so they stay at the same voltage. Together they protect people from electric shock, let breakers trip quickly on faults and reduce electrical noise that can upset sensitive electronics. Lightning protection and surge protectors stop sudden voltage spikes from damaging equipment.

From earth electrode to equipment. One continuous, low-impedance bonding network keeps every metal part at the same potential.

Think of it like…

Bonding is like tying all the boats in a harbour together: when a wave comes, they all rise and fall together, so nobody gets crushed between two boats at different heights.

Real-world example

At the fictional Pinewood Data, a technician touching two racks on different circuits feels a small tingle. An investigation finds one rack was never bonded to the room's bonding network. After connecting it with a green-and-yellow bonding conductor to the row's bonding busbar, the voltage difference measures near zero. The team then adds rack bonding to its installation checklist.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An earth electrode system (rods, rings or mesh) connects the site's electrical system to the ground.
  2. The main earthing terminal or primary bonding busbar links incoming services, structural steel and electrical earth.
  3. Bonding conductors connect racks, cable trays, pipes and raised floor pedestals to a common bonding network.
  4. Surge protective devices divert voltage spikes from lightning or switching to earth.
  5. Engineers test earth resistance and continuity regularly and after any building works.

Who uses it

Electrical engineers, telecommunications installers, lightning-protection specialists and commissioning engineers handle grounding and bonding.

Key takeaway

Remember the difference: grounding/earthing connects to the earth; bonding connects metal parts to each other. Both matter for safety.

Going deeper

  • IEC earthing codes use letters: the first (T or I) gives the source's relation to earth, the second (T or N) the exposed parts, and -S, -C or -C-S whether neutral and protective conductors are separate or combined.
  • Fast fault clearing needs a low earth fault loop impedance: the lower Zs, the higher the fault current and the sooner the breaker's instantaneous trip operates.
  • TIA-607 defines the telecom bonding hierarchy (PBB, TBB, SBB) and requires bonding conductors to be correctly sized, labelled and routed as directly as possible.
  • Surge protection is layered: Type 1 SPDs at the service entrance for lightning currents, Type 2 at distribution boards and Type 3 close to sensitive equipment.
  • Earth electrode resistance is measured by fall-of-potential or clamp-on methods; targets of a few ohms are common, but local codes and the design set the requirement.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Installing a separate 'clean' earth rod for IT equipment: unbonded earths create dangerous voltage differences and breach wiring codes.
  • Bonding racks through painted surfaces without proper lugs or jumpers, leaving high-resistance connections.
  • Treating grounding as a one-off job: alterations, corrosion and new racks require periodic continuity and resistance testing.

docs.title: Try it: Simple earth-loop check: will a breaker trip fast enough? (TN system)
docs.text:
u0 = 230            # nominal voltage to earth (V)
zs = 0.8            # measured earth fault loop impedance (ohms)
fault_a = u0 / zs
mcb_instant_trip = 5 * 32   # Type B 32 A MCB trips instantly at 3-5 x In
print(f"Fault current {fault_a:.0f} A ->", "trips fast" if fault_a >= mcb_instant_trip else "TOO SLOW: investigate")
